title: R Companion
text:
Welcome
This companion shows you how to use R to get the graphs and values each textbook chapter covers, for your coursework and for your own research. You do not need any coding experience, and you do not need to become an R programmer. You need to copy our code, change a few marked lines, and run it.
The textbook explains the statistics; this companion explains the clicks and the code. Each companion chapter matches the textbook chapter with the same number.

title: R Companion
text:
How to use each chapter

Read the textbook chapter first.
Download the chapter’s script and the dataset into one folder on your computer.
Open the script in RStudio and run it, following along with the companion chapter. Your output should match what you see here.
To use your own data, find the lines marked # CHANGE THIS: and put in your dataset and variables.

title: R Companion
text:
Before you start
If R and RStudio are not on your computer yet, start with Getting Set Up. If you cannot install software (for example, on a Chromebook or a library computer), the same chapter shows you how to use RStudio in a web browser instead.

title: Getting Set Up
text:
Install R
This chapter gets R working on your computer. By the end, you will have run your first script, read a dataset, and loaded a package.
You need two free programs:
Install R first, then RStudio. If you cannot install software on your computer, skip to Using RStudio in a web browser and use RStudio in your web browser instead.
Choose your computer’s operating system. The choice applies to every set of tabs in this chapter.

title: Getting Set Up
text:
WindowsMac



Go to https://cran.r-project.org.
Click Download R for Windows, then base, then the Download R link at the top of the page (it includes a version number, such as R-4.5.1).
Open the downloaded file. If Windows asks whether to allow this app to make changes to your device, click Yes.
Click Next on every screen to accept the standard settings, then Finish.




Find out which kind of chip your Mac has: open the Apple menu, choose About This Mac, and look at the line labeled Chip or Processor. It says either “Apple” (M1, M2, and so on) or “Intel.”



The About This Mac window, with the chip listed.


Go to https://cran.r-project.org and click Download R for macOS.
Download the .pkg file that matches your chip: the one labeled for Apple silicon (arm64) if your chip says Apple, or the one labeled for Intel (x86_64) if it says Intel.
Open the downloaded file and click Continue through each screen, then Install. Enter your Mac password if asked.







NoteYou do not need XQuartz



The R download page mentions XQuartz, a program that a few specialized packages need. Nothing in this companion uses it, so you can skip it.








WarningCommon error: R will not install or will not open



What you see: the installer stops with a message that the software cannot be installed, or R installs but will not open.
What it means: you most likely downloaded the version for the other kind of chip.
How to fix it: check your chip again (step 1), download the matching file, and install it.

title: Getting Set Up
text:
Install RStudio

WindowsMac



Go to https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/.
Skip the “Install R” step on that page (you just did it) and click the button to download RStudio Desktop for Windows.
Open the downloaded file, click Yes if Windows asks for permission, and click Next through each screen, then Finish.
Open RStudio from the Start menu.




Go to https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/.
Skip the “Install R” step on that page (you just did it) and click the button to download RStudio Desktop for macOS.
Open the downloaded .dmg file. A window opens showing the RStudio icon and your Applications folder.
Drag the RStudio icon onto the Applications folder.
Open your Applications folder and double-click RStudio. If your Mac asks whether you are sure you want to open an app downloaded from the internet, click Open.




The RStudio installer window on a Mac.








WarningCommon error: RStudio disappears after a restart



What you see: RStudio worked yesterday, but today you cannot find it.
What it means: RStudio was opened straight from the downloaded .dmg window instead of being copied into Applications first.
How to fix it: open the .dmg file again, drag RStudio onto the Applications folder, and from now on open it from Applications.











WarningCommon error: you opened R instead of RStudio



What you see: a plain window with a few lines of text about the R version and copyright, and a > symbol, but none of the panes described below.



The plain R window, which looks like a terminal.


What it means: both programs are now on your computer, and you opened R by mistake.
How to fix it: close that window and open RStudio. You never need to open R yourself; RStudio starts it for you.

Where R runs your code and prints the results.

The datasets and values R is holding right now.


Lower right

Your folders, your graphs, your packages, and R’s help pages, each on its own tab.

title: Getting Set Up
section: Make a folder for your work
text:
Make a folder for your work
Make one folder for everything in this course, for example a folder called Stats R inside Documents. Save every dataset and every script into it. When R looks for a file, it looks in one folder at a time, so keeping everything together prevents most “file not found” problems.






WarningCommon error: the downloaded file has a different name



What you see: the file in your folder is called census_at_school (1).csv or census_at_school.csv.csv instead of census_at_school.csv.
What it means: your browser added (1) because you downloaded the file twice, or Windows is hiding the .csv ending and you typed it in again while renaming.
How to fix it: rename the file so it matches the name in the script exactly. If Excel opens the file after you download it, close Excel without saving, since saving from Excel can change the file.

title: Getting Set Up
text:
Your first script
A script is a text file of R code that you can save, rerun, and change later.

In RStudio, choose File > New File > R Script. The Source pane opens in the upper left.
Type this line into it:
2 + 2
With your cursor on that line, press Ctrl + Enter (Windows) or Cmd + Return (Mac). You can also click the Run button at the top of the Source pane.
Look in the Console. R prints the answer:
[1] 4
The [1] only means “first value.” The answer is 4.



A script containing 2+2, after running it, with the answer in the Console.


Save the script with File > Save, into your course folder, with a name like practice.R.

To run a single line, put your cursor on it and press Ctrl + Enter or Cmd + Return. To run several lines, highlight them first and then press the same keys.






WarningCommon error: a + sign in the Console instead of an answer



What you see
> mean(c(1, 2, 3)
+
What it means: the > symbol means R is ready for a new command. A + at the start of the line means R is still waiting for the end of the last one, usually a closing parenthesis ) or quotation mark " that is missing.
How to fix it: click in the Console and press Esc to cancel. Then fix the line in your script so every ( has a matching ) and every " has a partner, and run it again.

title: Getting Set Up
text:
Set the working directory
The working directory is the folder where R looks for files. Point it at your course folder every time you open RStudio:

Make sure your script is saved in your course folder.
Choose Session > Set Working Directory > To Source File Location.

To check, type list.files() in the Console and press Enter. R lists the files in your working directory, and your dataset should be among them.



The Session menu with Set Working Directory expanded.

title: Getting Set Up
text:
Install and load packages
A package is a free add-on that gives R new abilities, such as drawing graphs. There are two steps, and they are easy to mix up:

Install a package once, the same way you install an app on your phone.
Load a package every time you open RStudio, the same way you open the app each time you use it.

To install the packages this companion uses, copy this line into the Console (not your script) and press Enter:
install.packages(c("ggplot2", "psych", "car", "effectsize",
                   "emmeans", "pROC", "forecast", "DescTools"))
c() combines several names into one list, so one command installs all eight packages. The command runs across two lines; copy both lines together.
R downloads the packages and prints many lines of progress, which can take a few minutes. When the > symbol returns, it is done. You never need to run this line again on this computer.






NoteQuestions R may ask while installing




“Would you like to use a personal library instead?” Type yes and press Enter, both times if it asks twice.
“Do you want to install from sources the packages which need compilation?” Type no and press Enter.
On Windows, a warning that Rtools is required can be ignored. You do not need Rtools.



To load a package, put a library() line at the top of your script. Every chapter script already starts with the lines it needs:
library(ggplot2)
Notice that install.packages() needs quotation marks around the name and library() does not.






WarningCommon error: there is no package called …



What you see

library(ggplot2x)

Error in `library()`:
! there is no package called 'ggplot2x'


What it means: the package is not installed (or its name is misspelled, as it is here).
How to fix it: check the spelling, then run install.packages("ggplot2") in the Console with the correct name, and run the library() line again.








WarningCommon error: could not find function …



What you see
> ggplot(students, aes(x = Sleep1))
Error in ggplot(students, aes(x = Sleep1)) :
  could not find function "ggplot"
What it means: the package is installed but not loaded. This happens when you open RStudio and run a graph before running the library() line.
How to fix it: run the library() lines at the top of the script first, then run your graph again.

title: Getting Set Up
text:
Read a dataset
Download census_at_school.csv into your course folder. Then type this line into your script and run it:

students <- read.csv("census_at_school.csv")

This line reads the file and stores it under the name students. The <- arrow means “store what is on the right under the name on the left.” In the Environment pane, students now appears with 500 obs. of 35 variables: 500 rows (students) and 35 columns (variables).
{fig-alt=“RStudio after running students <- read.csv(”census_at_school.csv”). The script is in the Source pane. In the Environment pane at upper right, a red arrow points to the new line students, 500 obs. of 35 variables.”}






NoteShortcut for the arrow



Press Alt and the minus key together (Windows) or Option and the minus key (Mac) to type <- in one step.








WarningCommon error: cannot open file … No such file or directory



What you see

students <- read.csv("census_at_scool.csv")

Warning in file(file, "rt"): cannot open file 'census_at_scool.csv': No such
file or directory


Error in `file()`:
! cannot open the connection


What it means: R looked in your working directory and did not find a file with that exact name.
How to fix it: check three things, in this order:

The file name in your script is spelled exactly right, including .csv and the quotation marks (this example is missing an “h”).
The working directory is set (Session > Set Working Directory > To Source File Location).
The file is really in your course folder: run list.files() and look for it.



You are set up. Continue to Chapter 1 to make your first graph.

title: Getting Set Up
section: Using RStudio in a web browser (Posit Cloud)
text:
Using RStudio in a web browser (Posit Cloud)
If you cannot install R on your computer (for example, a Chromebook, a tablet with a keyboard, or a computer you do not own), you can use Posit Cloud, which runs RStudio in a web browser. Everything in this companion works the same way there, with two differences, noted below.

Go to https://posit.cloud and sign up for a free account.
Click New Project, then New RStudio Project. RStudio opens in your browser after a short wait.
To add a dataset or script, click Upload in the Files pane (lower right), choose the file, and click OK.
Install the packages with the install.packages() line from Install and load packages.

The two differences:

You do not need to set the working directory. The project folder already is the working directory, so uploaded files are found automatically.
Packages are installed once per project, not once per computer. If you start a new project, install the packages again. Using one project for the whole course avoids this.

The free plan limits how many hours per month you can use Posit Cloud; check the current limits on its website. Save your scripts often, and download them (Files pane, More > Export) to keep a copy.

title: 1  Graphs and Summaries
text:
1.1 The data
In this chapter you will make five of the graphs from Chapter 1 of the textbook (a bar chart, a histogram, side-by-side box plots, and two scatterplots) and calculate a mean and a median.
Every graph in this chapter uses the same recipe, so once you have made the first one, the rest are small changes to it.
Get the script: Download the Chapter 1 script, chapter_01.R, and save it in the same folder as your data. It holds all of the code in this chapter, so you can run each piece as you read instead of typing it.
The examples use census_at_school.csv, a sample of 500 high school seniors in Pennsylvania. Download census_at_school.csv into the same folder as the script. To use your own dataset, you will copy the steps here and change the marked lines.
The variables used in this chapter:

title: 1  Graphs and Summaries
text:
Variables from census_at_school.csv used in this chapter







Variable
Type
What it records




GetToSchool

Main mode of transportation used to get to school (Bus, Car, or Walk, where Walk includes bicycles and skateboards).


Sleep1

The typical number of hours of sleep the student gets on a school night.


TravelTime
Numerical
The time it takes the student to travel to school, recorded in minutes.

The student’s armspan measured in centimeters.

The student’s height measured in centimeters.

The individual’s gender (Female or Male).

title: 1  Graphs and Summaries
section: 1.2 Load the package and the data
text:
1.2 Load the package and the data
Start every script the same way: load the packages, then read the data. If you have not installed ggplot2 yet, go back to Install and load packages in Getting Set Up.

# Load ggplot2, the package that draws our graphs. You install it
# once (see Getting Set Up), but you load it every time you open
# RStudio.
library(ggplot2)


# Read the CSV file and store it under the name "students".
# CHANGE THIS: the file name of your dataset, inside the quotes.
students <- read.csv("census_at_school.csv")

# List the variable names, so you can check that the data loaded
# and see exactly how each name is spelled.
names(students)

 [1] "Year"           "Gender"         "Age"           
 [4] "Hand"           "Height"         "Foot"          
 [7] "Armspan"        "Languages"      "GetToSchool"   
[10] "TravelTime"     "ReactionTime"   "MemoryScore"   
[13] "Activity"       "Music"          "BirthMonth"    
[16] "Season"         "Allergies"      "Vegetarian"    
[19] "FavFood"        "FavDrink"       "FavSubject"    
[22] "Sleep1"         "Sleep2"         "Occupants"     
[25] "Communicate"    "TextsSent"      "HangHours"     
[28] "HWHours"        "VideoGameHours" "ComputerHours" 
[31] "TVHours"        "WorkHours"      "SchoolPressure"
[34] "Superpower"     "Preference"    


The <- arrow stores the data under the name students. From now on, students means “the whole dataset.” The list of names is your spelling reference: R treats Sleep1 and sleep1 as two different things, so copy names exactly as they appear here.






TipWith your own data



Change the file name inside the quotes to your dataset’s file name, such as "student_lifestyle_sleep.csv". You can keep the name students, or choose a name that describes your data (if you do, change it everywhere it appears). Run names(students) again and keep the new list handy; the variable names in the graphs below will change to match it.

title: 1  Graphs and Summaries
text:
1.3 Picking out one variable with $
Many R commands work on one variable at a time. The $ sign picks one variable (one column) out of a dataset: students$TravelTime means “the TravelTime column of students.” Read it as “students, the TravelTime column.”

# The $ sign picks one variable (column) out of a dataset:
# students$TravelTime means "the TravelTime column of students".
# head() shows only the first six values, so the screen does not
# fill up with all 500.
head(students$TravelTime)

[1]  5 15  4  9  8  7


These are the travel times, in minutes, of the first six students in the dataset.
You will use $ with commands such as mean() and median(). Inside ggplot() you do not need it: you name the dataset once at the start, and ggplot() looks up each variable name in that dataset.






WarningCommon error: NULL



What you see

head(students$travelTime)

NULL


What it means: NULL means “nothing there.” R found no column called travelTime (with a lowercase “t”), so it has nothing to show. R does not stop with an error here, which makes this one easy to miss.
How to fix it: check the spelling after the $ against names(students).

title: 1  Graphs and Summaries
text:
1.4 Bar chart
A bar chart shows how many observations fall in each category of a categorical variable.

# 1. BAR CHART: one bar per category. The height of each bar is
#    the number of students in that category.
#    ggplot(students, ...) names the dataset to use.
#    aes() says which variable goes where; x = puts it on the
#      horizontal axis. (aes is short for "aesthetics".)
#    geom_bar() draws the bars. fill = sets the color inside the
#      bars, and color = sets the color of their outlines.
#    labs() writes the title and the axis labels. Anything inside
#      quotes is printed exactly as you type it.
#    theme_minimal() gives the graph a plain background.
#      base_size = 14 sets the text size, in points. You can leave
#      it as is.
# CHANGE THIS: your categorical variable after x =
ggplot(students, aes(x = GetToSchool)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#0072B2", color = "black") +
  # CHANGE THIS: your title and x-axis label, inside the quotes
  labs(title = "How Students Get to School",
       x = "Way of getting to school",
       y = "Number of students") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)




Bar chart of how students get to school.




Every graph in this companion is built from the same four parts, joined with + signs:

ggplot(students, aes(x = GetToSchool)) names the data and the variable to plot.
geom_bar() says what kind of graph to draw. Each graph type has its own geom_ (you will see geom_histogram(), geom_boxplot(), and geom_point() next).
labs() writes the title and axis labels. Anything inside quotes is printed as you typed it.
theme_minimal(base_size = 14) gives a plain background and readable text.

The settings inside the parentheses, such as fill = "#0072B2" and base_size = 14, are called arguments. The comments in the script explain each one, including the ones you can leave as they are.






NoteAbout the colors



Codes such as "#0072B2" (blue) and "#D55E00" (vermillion, a red-orange) come from the Okabe-Ito palette, the same colors the textbook uses. They were chosen so that people with color blindness can tell them apart. The top of the script lists more of them. You can also type a plain color name, such as "darkgreen".








WarningCommon error: object not found



What you see

ggplot(students, aes(x = gettoschool)) +
  geom_bar()

Error in `geom_bar()`:
! Problem while computing aesthetics.
ℹ Error occurred in the 1st layer.
Caused by error:
! object 'gettoschool' not found


What it means: R could not find a variable called gettoschool. The real name is GetToSchool, with capital letters.
How to fix it: copy the variable name exactly from the names(students) list, including capital letters, numbers, and underscores.








WarningCommon error: Cannot use + with a single argument



What you see

ggplot(students, aes(x = Sleep1))







  + geom_histogram()

Error:
! Cannot use `+` with a single argument.
ℹ Did you accidentally put `+` on a new line?


What it means: the + has to come at the end of a line. When a line ends without +, R thinks the command is finished, draws an empty graph, and then does not know what to do with the + on the next line.
How to fix it: move each + to the end of the line above it, as in the examples.

title: 1  Graphs and Summaries
text:
1.5 Histogram
A histogram shows the shape of a numerical variable. Use it to describe shape (Chapter 1 of the textbook covers skew and floor and ceiling effects).

# 2. HISTOGRAM: shows the shape of one numerical variable.
#    binwidth = 1 makes each bar 1 unit wide, in the units of your
#      variable (here, 1 hour of sleep).
#    fill = and color = work the same way as in the bar chart.
# CHANGE THIS: your numerical variable after x =
ggplot(students, aes(x = Sleep1)) +
  # CHANGE THIS: a binwidth that suits your variable
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "#0072B2", color = "black") +
  # CHANGE THIS: your title and x-axis label, inside the quotes
  labs(title = "Hours of Sleep on a School Night",
       x = "Hours of sleep",
       y = "Number of students") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)




Histogram of hours of sleep on a school night.




binwidth sets how wide each bar is, in the units of your variable. Here each bar covers 1 hour of sleep.






NoteMessage: Pick better value with binwidth



If you leave out binwidth, R picks 30 bars on its own and prints this message:
`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value with `binwidth`.
This is a message, not an error; the graph still draws. Adding binwidth removes the message and usually gives a clearer graph.








TipWith your own data



Change Sleep1 to your numerical variable, and update the title and x-axis label. Choose a binwidth in your variable’s units: 1 works for counts such as classes missed, but a GPA needs something smaller, such as 0.25. Try a few values and keep the one that shows the shape best. For a second variable, copy the whole block and change it again.

title: 1  Graphs and Summaries
text:
1.6 Mean and median
mean() and median() each take one variable, picked out with the $ sign.

# 3. MEAN AND MEDIAN of one numerical variable. Each one takes a
#    single variable, picked out with the $ sign.
# CHANGE THIS: your variable after the $, in both lines
mean(students$TravelTime)

[1] 11.324

median(students$TravelTime)

[1] 9


The average travel time is about 11.3 minutes, and the median is 9 minutes. The number after [1] is the answer (the [1] only means “first value”).






WarningCommon error: the answer is NA



What you see

# Armspan has some empty cells, so mean() gives NA.
mean(students$Armspan)

[1] NA


What it means: NA stands for “not available.” Some students left Armspan blank, and R will not average a column with blanks in it unless you tell it to skip them.
How to fix it: add na.rm = TRUE (“NA remove”) inside the parentheses.

# na.rm = TRUE removes the empty cells before R calculates.
# (na.rm is short for "NA remove"; TRUE means yes.)
mean(students$Armspan, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 169.8084

median(students$Armspan, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 169


A misspelled variable name also gives NA, with a warning:

mean(students$sleep1)

Warning in mean.default(students$sleep1): argument is not numeric
or logical: returning NA


[1] NA


If you see this warning, check the spelling against names(students).








TipWith your own data



Change TravelTime to your variable in both lines. If either answer is NA, your variable has blank cells; add na.rm = TRUE as shown in the box above.

title: 1  Graphs and Summaries
text:
1.7 Side-by-side box plots
Side-by-side box plots compare a numerical variable across groups. This one compares school-night sleep for the two survey years.

# 4. SIDE-BY-SIDE BOX PLOTS: one box per group.
#    Year is stored as a number (2023 or 2024). factor() tells R
#    to treat it as group names, which gives one box per year.
#    y = puts the numerical variable on the vertical axis.
#    fill = sets the color inside the boxes.
# CHANGE THIS: your group variable inside factor(), and your
#              numerical variable after y =
ggplot(students, aes(x = factor(Year), y = Sleep1)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#0072B2") +
  # CHANGE THIS: your title and axis labels, inside the quotes
  labs(title = "School-Night Sleep by Survey Year",
       x = "Survey year",
       y = "Hours of sleep") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)




Box plots of school-night sleep for each survey year.




Year is stored as a number, but it is a categorical variable: 2023 and 2024 are group names, not amounts. Wrapping it in factor() tells R to treat it as groups.






WarningCommon error: only one box appears



What you see

ggplot(students, aes(x = Year, y = Sleep1)) +
  geom_boxplot()

Warning: Orientation is not uniquely specified when both the x and y
aesthetics are continuous. Picking default orientation 'x'.


Warning: Continuous x aesthetic
ℹ did you forget `aes(group = ...)`?









What it means: without factor(), R reads Year as an ordinary number and draws one box for everyone. The warning about aes(group = ...) is R’s hint that something is off.
How to fix it: wrap the group variable in factor(), as in aes(x = factor(Year), y = Sleep1).








TipWith your own data



Put your group variable inside factor() and your numerical variable after y =, then update the labels. If your groups are stored as numbers (for example, a class year coded 1 to 4), you need factor(). If they are stored as words, such as Bus and Car, factor() does no harm, so you can always keep it.

title: 1  Graphs and Summaries
text:
1.8 Scatterplot
A scatterplot shows how two numerical variables move together, with one dot per student.

# 5. SCATTERPLOT: one dot per student, showing how two numerical
#    variables move together. The variable after x = goes on the
#    horizontal axis; the variable after y = goes on the vertical
#    axis.
#    geom_point() draws the dots. color = sets their color.
# CHANGE THIS: your x variable and your y variable
ggplot(students, aes(x = Height, y = Armspan)) +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2") +
  # CHANGE THIS: your title and axis labels, inside the quotes
  labs(title = "Height and Armspan",
       x = "Height (cm)",
       y = "Armspan (cm)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

Warning: Removed 34 rows containing missing values or values outside the
scale range (`geom_point()`).





Scatterplot of armspan against height.




The variable after x = goes on the horizontal axis, and the variable after y = goes on the vertical axis.






NoteWarning: Removed 34 rows containing missing values



R prints this warning because 34 students have a blank Armspan, so it has no place to put their dots. The graph is still correct; it just shows the 466 students with both measurements. With your own data, the number in the warning tells you how many rows were left out.








TipWith your own data



Change both variables and all three labels. Put the variable you think of as the explanation (the predictor) after x =, and the outcome after y =.

title: 1  Graphs and Summaries
text:
1.9 Scatterplot with groups
Adding a third variable takes two more words inside aes(). Here each gender gets its own color and its own shape, so the groups can be told apart in black and white or by readers who do not see color differences.

# 6. SCATTERPLOT WITH GROUPS: the same graph, with each group in
#    its own color AND its own shape. The shapes let a reader tell
#    the groups apart even in black and white.
#    color = and shape = inside aes() name the group variable.
#    scale_color_manual(values = ...) picks the colors, one per
#      group, in alphabetical order of the group names (here,
#      Female gets blue and Male gets vermillion). c() combines
#      the colors into one list. With more groups, add more colors
#      from the list at the top of this script.

title: 2  Proportions and Reliability
text:
2.3 A proportion for one variable
A proportion is the share of observations in one category: the count in that category divided by the total. Start by counting with table():

# 1. COUNT AND PROPORTION FOR ONE VARIABLE.
#    table() counts how many rows have each value. Here 0 means
#    "no" and 1 means "yes, rode with a driver who had been
#    drinking".
# CHANGE THIS: your categorical variable after the $
ride_counts <- table(youth$ride.alc.driver)
ride_counts


   0    1 
9210 4177 

# prop.table() turns the counts into proportions (each count
# divided by the total), so the proportions add up to 1.
# round(..., 3) rounds them to 3 decimal places.
round(prop.table(ride_counts), 3)


    0     1 
0.688 0.312 


The first table gives the counts: 9,210 students answered 0 (no) and 4,177 answered 1 (yes). The second gives the proportions: 0.312, or about 31.2%, of these students rode with a driver who had been drinking.
The names on top of each table (0 and 1) are the codes stored in the data. Check the dataset’s key to see what each code means.
For a variable coded 0 and 1, the mean is the same as the proportion of 1s, which gives you a one-line shortcut:

# Shortcut for a variable coded 0 and 1: its mean is the
# proportion of 1s.
mean(youth$ride.alc.driver)

[1] 0.3120191








TipWith your own data



Change ride.alc.driver to your categorical variable. table() works for any number of categories and for categories stored as words, such as Bus, Car, and Walk. The mean() shortcut works only for a variable coded 0 and 1; if it gives NA, add na.rm = TRUE as in Chapter 1.

title: 2  Proportions and Reliability
text:
2.4 Proportions for two groups
To compare a proportion across groups, count every combination of the two variables. Put the group variable first (it becomes the rows) and the outcome second (it becomes the columns):

# 2. PROPORTIONS FOR TWO GROUPS.
#    table(rows, columns) counts every combination of two
#    variables. The first variable becomes the rows and the second
#    becomes the columns. Here smoke is 0 = never tried smoking,
#    1 = has tried smoking.
# CHANGE THIS: your group variable first, then your outcome
ride_by_smoke <- table(youth$smoke, youth$ride.alc.driver)
ride_by_smoke

   
       0    1
  0 4940 1113
  1 4027 2919

# margin = 1 divides each row by its own row total, so each row
# adds up to 1. That gives the proportion of "yes" answers within
# each group.
round(prop.table(ride_by_smoke, margin = 1), 3)

   
        0     1
  0 0.816 0.184
  1 0.580 0.420


In the first table, the rows are smoke (0 = never tried smoking, 1 = has tried smoking) and the columns are ride.alc.driver (0 = no, 1 = yes). In the second table, each row adds up to 1. Read across a row: among students who had never tried smoking, 0.184 (18.4%) rode with a driver who had been drinking; among students who had tried smoking, 0.420 (42.0%) did.






WarningCommon error: the rows do not add up to 1



What you see

round(prop.table(ride_by_smoke, margin = 2), 3)

   
        0     1
  0 0.551 0.276
  1 0.449 0.724


What it means: margin = 2 divides by the column totals, so each column adds up to 1 instead of each row. These numbers answer a different question (“of the students who rode with a drinking driver, what share had smoked?”).
How to fix it: use margin = 1, and put the group variable first inside table(), so each row is one group.








NoteBlank cells are left out



table() skips blank cells without telling you. Here 388 students left smoke blank, so the two-group table counts 12,999 students instead of 13,387. Add the counts in a table to see how many rows it used.








TipWith your own data



Put your group variable first and your outcome variable second inside table(), and keep margin = 1.

title: 2  Proportions and Reliability
text:
2.5 Cronbach’s alpha
Cronbach’s alpha checks whether a set of survey items measures one thing consistently enough to add the items together. Read the anxiety data, then pick out the items that belong to one scale. The AMAS has two parts; this example uses the five items on anxiety about learning math.

# Read the math anxiety survey and store it under the name
# "anxiety".
# CHANGE THIS: the file name of your dataset, inside the quotes.
anxiety <- read.csv("amas_math_anxiety.csv")
names(anxiety)

[1] "item_1" "item_2" "item_3" "item_4" "item_5" "item_6" "item_7"
[8] "item_8" "item_9"



# 3. CRONBACH'S ALPHA.
#    First, pick out the survey items that belong to one scale.
#    Square brackets choose part of a dataset: [rows, columns].
#    Leaving the space before the comma empty means "all rows".
#    c() combines the column names into one list.
#    Here we use the five "learning anxiety" items.
# CHANGE THIS: the names of your items, each inside quotes
learning_items <- anxiety[, c("item_1", "item_3", "item_6",
                              "item_7", "item_9")]
head(learning_items)

  item_1 item_3 item_6 item_7 item_9
1      5      5      5      5      5
2      2      2      2      2      2
3      1      1      1      1      1
4      1      2      2      4      4
5      2      1      1      1      3
6      2      2      2      2      2


The square brackets choose part of a dataset. Inside them, the space before the comma picks rows and the part after the comma picks columns. Leaving the row part empty keeps every row, so anxiety[, c("item_1", "item_3")] means “all rows, just these two columns.”






WarningCommon error: object ‘item_1’ not found

anxiety[, c(item_1, item_3)]

Error:
! object 'item_1' not found


What it means: without quotation marks, R looks for something stored under the name item_1, finds nothing, and stops.
How to fix it: put each column name inside quotation marks, as in c("item_1", "item_3").

# psych::alpha() means "the alpha() function from the psych
# package". Writing psych:: in front makes sure R uses the right

R prints a lot. The two places to look:

What you see (the list of numbers is much longer)
Error: Unknown colour name: c(5, 2, 1, 1, 2, 2, 4, 1, 1, 1, ...
What it means: you wrote alpha() without psych:: in front, and R used the alpha() from ggplot2, which sets how see-through a color is. It has nothing to do with Cronbach’s alpha.
How to fix it: write psych::alpha(), as in the script.








WarningCommon error: items were negatively correlated



What you see

# A copy of the items with item_1 flipped, so 1 becomes 5 and
# 5 becomes 1, to show the warning.
flipped_items <- learning_items
flipped_items$item_1 <- 6 - flipped_items$item_1
psych::alpha(flipped_items)

Warning in psych::alpha(flipped_items): Some items were negatively correlated with the first principal component and probably 
should be reversed.  
To do this, run the function again with the 'check.keys=TRUE' option


What it means: one item runs in the opposite direction from the others. This happens when a survey includes items worded the other way (for example, “I feel calm during math tests”), where a high score means low anxiety. Left as is, the item pulls alpha down (in this example, to about 0.59).
How to fix it: reverse the item before calculating alpha. For a 1 to 5 scale, subtract each answer from 6, as in items$item_1 <- 6 - items$item_1, so 1 becomes 5 and 5 becomes 1. For a 1 to 7 scale, subtract from 8.








TipWith your own data



Put your item names inside c(), each in quotation marks, and give the set a name that describes it. Report the raw_alpha value from the first table.

title: 2  Proportions and Reliability
text:
2.6 Composite score
Once alpha shows the items fit together, add each person’s answers into one score. rowSums() adds across each row, and the <- arrow stores the result as a new column in the dataset:

# 4. COMPOSITE SCORE: add each person's answers across the items.
#    rowSums() adds across each row. The <- arrow stores the
#    result as a new column called learning_score in the dataset.
# CHANGE THIS: a name for your new score after the $, and the name
#              of your items inside rowSums()
anxiety$learning_score <- rowSums(learning_items)

# Check the new scores: the first six, then the mean.
head(anxiety$learning_score)

[1] 25 10  5 13  8 10

mean(anxiety$learning_score)

[1] 8.907727


Each person now has a learning anxiety score from 5 (an answer of 1 on all five items) to 25 (an answer of 5 on all five). The average is about 8.9. The new column works like any other: use anxiety$learning_score in mean(), or put learning_score in a ggplot() histogram from Chapter 1.






TipWith your own data



Choose a name for the new score after the $, and put the items you checked with alpha inside rowSums(). If any item has blank cells, rowSums() gives NA for those people; add na.rm = TRUE only if your study’s instructions say to score people with missing answers.

section: 3.2 Load the package and the data
text:
3.2 Load the package and the data
The t-tests are built into R. Cohen’s d comes from the effectsize package; if you have not installed it yet, go back to Install and load packages in Getting Set Up.

# Load effectsize, the package that calculates Cohen's d. The
# t-tests themselves are built into R and need no package.
library(effectsize)


# CHANGE THIS: the file name of your dataset, inside the quotes.
students <- read.csv("census_at_school.csv")

Before any t-test, check the shape of your variable with a histogram (Chapter 1) to judge whether the test’s requirements are met, as the textbook describes.
crumbs: 3  t-Tests, Effect Sizes, and Power

title: 3  t-Tests, Effect Sizes, and Power
text:
3.3 Single sample t-test
A single sample t-test compares the mean of one variable to a fixed benchmark. Here the question is whether high school seniors sleep a different amount on school nights than the 8 hours often recommended for teenagers.

# 1. SINGLE SAMPLE t-test: compares the mean of one variable to a
#    fixed number (a benchmark).
#    The first argument is the variable to test.
#    mu = 8 is the benchmark: here, 8 hours of sleep. (mu is the
#      Greek letter for a population mean.)
# CHANGE THIS: your variable after the $, and your benchmark
#              after mu =
t.test(students$Sleep1, mu = 8)


    One Sample t-test

data:  students$Sleep1
t = -23.577, df = 499, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 8
95 percent confidence interval:
 6.692417 6.893583
sample estimates:
mean of x 
    6.793 


Every t-test in R prints the same layout. Here is where to find each value you report:

Where each value appears in R’s t-test output







What you report
Where it is in the output
In this example

t =
\(-23.58\)


Degrees of freedom

below .001 (see the note below)

[6.69, 6.89]

The line alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 8 confirms R ran the two-sided test, with \(H_1\) using \(\neq\), so the test can find an effect in either direction. R does this unless you tell it otherwise, so leave that setting alone.






NoteReading p-value < 2.2e-16



2.2e-16 is R’s way of writing a very small number: move the decimal point 16 places to the left, so 0.00000000000000022. R does not print p-values smaller than this, so it writes < 2.2e-16 instead. In a report, write p < .001.
The same shorthand appears elsewhere: 5.9e-04 means 0.00059.








TipWith your own data



Change the variable after the $, and put your benchmark after mu =. The benchmark comes from outside your data: a published average, a clinical cutoff, or a value set before you collected the data.

title: 3  t-Tests, Effect Sizes, and Power
text:
3.4 Matched pair t-test
A matched pair t-test compares two measurements taken on the same people, such as before and after. Here each student reported their sleep on non-school nights (Sleep2) and on school nights (Sleep1).

# 2. MATCHED PAIR t-test: compares two measurements taken on the
#    same people. Here each student reported sleep on a
#    non-school night (Sleep2) and on a school night (Sleep1).
#    paired = TRUE tells R the two columns belong to the same
#      people, row by row.
#    R subtracts the second variable from the first, so the
#      difference here is Sleep2 minus Sleep1.
# CHANGE THIS: your two variables, in the order you want them
#              subtracted
t.test(students$Sleep2, students$Sleep1, paired = TRUE)


    Paired t-test

data:  students$Sleep2 and students$Sleep1
t = 27.467, df = 499, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 1.944218 2.243782
sample estimates:
mean difference 
          2.094 


R subtracts the second variable from the first, row by row. Here that is non-school-night sleep minus school-night sleep, so the mean difference of 2.09 means students sleep about 2 hours more on non-school nights. The values to report are in the same places as before.
This is the same test as running a single sample t-test on the difference scores with mu = 0. If your dataset already has a difference column (such as a “change” variable), you can test that column with the code from the previous section instead.






TipWith your own data



Put your two measurements in the order you want them subtracted: usually the later measurement first, so a positive difference means an increase. Both variables must come from the same people, in the same rows.
crumbs: 3  t-Tests, Effect Sizes, and Power

title: 3  t-Tests, Effect Sizes, and Power
text:
3.5 Group means and standard deviations
To report two groups in APA style, you need each group’s mean and standard deviation. tapply() splits a variable by group and calculates something for each part:

# CHANGE THIS: the file name of your dataset, inside the quotes.
weight <- read.csv("weight_loss_incentive.csv")


# 3. GROUP MEANS AND STANDARD DEVIATIONS, for reporting.
#    tapply(variable, groups, function) splits the variable by
#      group and applies the function (mean or sd) to each part.
#    na.rm = TRUE skips the blank cells, as in Chapter 1.
# CHANGE THIS: your numerical variable and your group variable
#              in both lines
tapply(weight$WeightLoss, weight$Group, mean, na.rm = TRUE)

  Control Incentive 
 3.921053 15.676471 

tapply(weight$WeightLoss, weight$Group, sd, na.rm = TRUE)

  Control Incentive 
 9.107785  9.413988 


The control group lost an average of 3.92 pounds and the incentive group lost 15.68 pounds.






TipWith your own data



Change the numerical variable and the group variable in both lines. The third argument is the calculation: mean, sd, or median (with no parentheses after it).
crumbs: 3  t-Tests, Effect Sizes, and Power

title: 3  t-Tests, Effect Sizes, and Power
text:
3.6 Welch’s independent sample t-test
An independent sample t-test compares the means of two separate groups. R runs Welch’s version unless you tell it otherwise. Welch’s version adjusts for groups with different spreads, so its p-value stays reliable whether or not the spreads match.

# 4. WELCH'S INDEPENDENT SAMPLE t-test: compares the means of two
#    separate groups. R uses Welch's version unless you tell it
#    otherwise.
#    WeightLoss ~ Group reads "WeightLoss, split by Group". The ~
#      sign (called a tilde) is on the top-left key of most
#      keyboards.
#    data = weight names the dataset, so you do not need $.
# CHANGE THIS: your numerical variable before the ~, your group
#              variable after it, and your dataset after data =
t.test(WeightLoss ~ Group, data = weight)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  WeightLoss by Group
t = -3.7982, df = 33.276, p-value = 0.0005889
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group Control and group Incentive is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -18.05026  -5.46058
sample estimates:
  mean in group Control mean in group Incentive 
               3.921053               15.676471 


The values to report are in the same places as before. Two things are new:

The degrees of freedom have decimals (33.28 here). That is normal for Welch’s test; report them as printed, rounded to two places.
The order of the groups: R puts the groups in alphabetical order (Control, then Incentive) and subtracts the second from the first. The confidence interval [\(-18.05\), \(-5.46\)] is negative because the control group lost less weight than the incentive group.

The ~ sign (called a tilde) means “split by”: WeightLoss ~ Group reads “WeightLoss, split by Group.” Because data = weight names the dataset, you do not need $.






WarningCommon error: grouping factor must have exactly 2 levels



What you see

t.test(Sleep1 ~ GetToSchool, data = students)

Error in `t.test.formula()`:
! grouping factor must have exactly 2 levels


What it means: a t-test compares exactly two groups, and GetToSchool has three (Bus, Car, and Walk).
How to fix it: keep only two groups first (see A t-test for one group only for how subset() works), or use a test built for three or more groups, the one-way ANOVA in Chapter 6.








TipWith your own data



Put your numerical variable before the ~, your group variable after it, and your dataset after data =. The group variable must have exactly two groups.
crumbs: 3  t-Tests, Effect Sizes, and Power

title: 3  t-Tests, Effect Sizes, and Power
text:
3.7 Cohen’s d
Cohen’s d measures how large the difference between the two groups is, in standard deviations. It is written the same way as the t-test:

# 5. COHEN'S d for the difference between the two groups. It is
#    written the same way as the t-test.
# CHANGE THIS: the same variables and dataset as your t-test
cohens_d(WeightLoss ~ Group, data = weight)

Warning: Missing values detected. NAs dropped.


Cohen's d |         95% CI
--------------------------
-1.27     | [-1.98, -0.54]

- Estimated using pooled SD.


Cohen’s d is \(-1.27\), a large effect by the usual rules of thumb (about 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium, and 0.8 large). As with the t-test, the sign only reflects the alphabetical order of the groups; judge the size from the number without its minus sign. The line Estimated using pooled SD means the standard deviation combines both groups, so the difference is measured against the spread of everyone in the study.






NoteWarning: Missing values detected. NAs dropped.



Two participants have a blank WeightLoss, so cohens_d() leaves them out and says so. The t-test leaves them out too, without saying anything.








TipWith your own data



Copy the variables and dataset from your t.test() line.

title: 3  t-Tests, Effect Sizes, and Power
section: 3.8 A t-test for one group only
text:
3.8 A t-test for one group only
Some questions are about one group: for example, whether the incentive group kept the weight off at the 7-month follow-up. First keep only that group’s rows with subset(), then test the smaller dataset.

# 6. A t-test FOR ONE GROUP ONLY.
#    subset() keeps only the rows that match a condition.
#    Group == "Incentive" means "Group is exactly Incentive". Use
#      two equals signs, and spell the group exactly as it appears
#      in the data, inside quotes.
#    The result is stored as a new, smaller dataset.
# CHANGE THIS: your dataset, your group variable, and the group
#              you want to keep
incentive <- subset(weight, Group == "Incentive")
nrow(incentive)

[1] 19

# Then test that group's Month7Loss against 0 (no change).
# CHANGE THIS: your variable after the $, and your benchmark
t.test(incentive$Month7Loss, mu = 0)


    One Sample t-test

data:  incentive$Month7Loss
t = 2.5054, df = 14, p-value = 0.0252
alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
  1.122724 14.477276
sample estimates:
mean of x 
      7.8 


The new dataset incentive has 19 rows, one per participant in the incentive group. They were still about 7.8 pounds lighter than at the start of the study, 95% CI [1.12, 14.48]. The degrees of freedom are 14, not 18, because 4 of these participants have a blank Month7Loss.






WarningCommon error: extra argument will be disregarded



What you see

wrong <- subset(weight, Group = "Incentive")

Warning: In subset.data.frame(weight, Group = "Incentive") :
 extra argument 'Group' will be disregarded

nrow(wrong)

[1] 38


What it means: with one equals sign, R does not compare anything. It ignores the condition and keeps all 38 rows, so any test on wrong uses both groups.
How to fix it: use two equals signs, ==, which means “is exactly.”








WarningCommon error: not enough ‘x’ observations



What you see

wrong <- subset(weight, Group == "incentive")
nrow(wrong)

[1] 0

t.test(wrong$Month7Loss, mu = 0)

Error in `t.test.default()`:
! not enough 'x' observations


What it means: no rows matched, so the new dataset is empty (0 rows) and there is nothing to test. The group is spelled Incentive, with a capital I.
How to fix it: copy the group name exactly as it appears in the data. To see the spellings, run table(weight$Group).








TipWith your own data



Change the dataset, the group variable, and the group name (inside quotes). Run nrow() on the result to check that the number of rows makes sense before you run the test.

title: 3  t-Tests, Effect Sizes, and Power
section: 3.9 Sample size for a power of 80%
text:
3.9 Sample size for a power of 80%
Before a study, a power analysis tells you how many participants you need. power.t.test() takes everything except the sample size and fills in the one value you leave out:

# 7. SAMPLE SIZE FOR 80% POWER (independent sample t-test).
#    delta = 0.5 is the effect size you expect, as a Cohen's d.
#    sd = 1 lets delta be read as a Cohen's d. Leave it at 1.
#    sig.level = 0.05 is the significance level (alpha).
#    power = 0.80 is the power you want.
#    R fills in the one value you leave out: here, n.
# CHANGE THIS: the effect size you expect, after delta =
power.t.test(delta = 0.5, sd = 1, sig.level = 0.05, power = 0.80)


     Two-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 63.76576
          delta = 0.5
             sd = 1
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8
    alternative = two.sided

NOTE: n is number in *each* group


To detect a medium effect (\(d = 0.5\)) with 80% power at \(\alpha = .05\), you need 63.77 participants in each group. Always round up: 64 per group, or 128 in total. The note at the bottom is a reminder that n counts one group, not the whole study.






TipWith your own data



Put the effect size you expect after delta =, as a Cohen’s d from past research or from the smallest effect that would matter in practice. If you know the effect in your variable’s own units instead (for example, a 4-point drop on a scale with a standard deviation of 11.5), put the raw difference after delta = and the standard deviation after sd =.

text:
Download census_at_school.csv, the high school survey from Chapter 1.
Download happy_planet_index_2024.csv, measurements for 147 countries, the dataset from the textbook chapter.



Variables used in this chapter







Variable
Dataset
What it records

section: 4.2 Load the package and the data
text:
4.2 Load the package and the data

library(ggplot2)


# CHANGE THIS: the file name of your dataset, inside the quotes.
students <- read.csv("census_at_school.csv")
crumbs: 4  Correlation and Simple Linear Regression

title: 4  Correlation and Simple Linear Regression
text:
4.3 Correlation
cor.test() calculates the linear correlation \(r\) between two numerical variables and tests whether the population correlation \(\rho\) is different from 0.

# 1. CORRELATION: cor.test() calculates r for two numerical
#    variables and tests whether the population correlation (rho)
#    is different from 0. The order of the two variables does not
#    matter.
# CHANGE THIS: your two numerical variables
cor.test(students$Height, students$Foot)


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  students$Height and students$Foot
t = 19.416, df = 498, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.6034251 0.7035770
sample estimates:
      cor 
0.6563834 


The output has the same layout as a t-test:

The correlation \(r\) is the number under cor at the bottom: 0.66, a large positive relationship between height and foot length by the usual social science guidelines (0.50 or higher is large).
The p-value is on the t = line. Here it is below .001 (see Reading p-value < 2.2e-16 in Chapter 3), so you reject \(H_0: \rho = 0\).
The 95% confidence interval for \(\rho\) is under 95 percent confidence interval: [0.60, 0.70].







TipWith your own data



Change the two variables. Draw their scatterplot first (Chapter 1) to check that the relationship looks like a straight line, because \(r\) only measures straight-line relationships. Blank cells are left out automatically.
crumbs: 4  Correlation and Simple Linear Regression

title: 4  Correlation and Simple Linear Regression
text:
4.4 Fit the regression line
lm() (short for “linear model”) fits the regression line. Store the model under a name so you can use it in the steps that follow, then print it with summary():

# 2. REGRESSION MODEL: lm() stands for "linear model".
#    Foot ~ Height reads "Foot, predicted by Height". The response
#      (y) goes before the ~ and the predictor (x) after it.
#    The model is stored under the name foot_model, so you can
#      use it in the steps below.
#    summary() prints the results.
# CHANGE THIS: your response variable, your predictor, your
#              dataset, and a name for your model
foot_model <- lm(Foot ~ Height, data = students)
summary(foot_model)


Call:
lm(formula = Foot ~ Height, data = students)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-6.4309 -1.1085 -0.0096  1.0860  7.2433 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -2.917007   1.437412  -2.029    0.043 *  
Height       0.162919   0.008391  19.416   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 1.909 on 498 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.4308,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.4297 
F-statistic:   377 on 1 and 498 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


The ~ works the same way as in Chapter 3. Put the response (\(y\)) before it and the predictor (\(x\)) after it: Foot ~ Height reads “Foot, predicted by Height.”
The summary is long. Here is where to find what you need:

Where each value appears in the regression summary







What you need
Where it is in the output
In this example




Intercept
(Intercept) row, Estimate column
\(-2.92\)


Slope
the predictor’s row (Height), Estimate column
0.163


p-value for the slope
the predictor’s row, last column, Pr(>|t|)
below .001


\(R^2\)
Multiple R-squared near the bottom
0.4308, or 43.1%



So the regression equation is: predicted foot length \(= -2.92 + 0.163 \times\) height. Each extra centimeter of height goes with a foot about 0.16 cm longer, and height explains 43.1% of the variation in foot length.






NoteThe stars and the scientific notation



The stars after each p-value (***) are R’s shorthand for how small the p-value is; the Signif. codes line underneath is their key. You can ignore them and report the p-value itself. <2e-16 is the same very small number explained in Chapter 3; report it as p < .001.








TipWith your own data



Change the response, the predictor, the dataset, and the model’s name. Use the same model name in every step below.
crumbs: 4  Correlation and Simple Linear Regression

title: 4  Correlation and Simple Linear Regression
text:
4.5 Scatterplot with the regression line
geom_smooth(method = "lm") adds the fitted line to a scatterplot:

# 3. SCATTERPLOT WITH THE REGRESSION LINE.
#    geom_smooth(method = "lm") adds the regression line.
#    se = FALSE leaves out the gray band around the line.
# CHANGE THIS: your predictor after x =, your response after y =,
#              and your labels
ggplot(students, aes(x = Height, y = Foot)) +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Foot Length and Height",
       x = "Height (cm)",
       y = "Foot length (cm)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'





Scatterplot of foot length against height, with the regression line.










NoteMessage: geom_smooth() using formula = ‘y ~ x’



This message only confirms that the line is a straight-line regression of your y variable on your x variable. You can ignore it.
crumbs: 4  Correlation and Simple Linear Regression

title: 4  Correlation and Simple Linear Regression
text:
4.6 Check the residuals
A residual is the actual value minus the predicted value. Store both as new columns in the dataset, so you can plot them:

# 4. RESIDUALS: store each student's predicted value and residual
#    (actual minus predicted) as two new columns in the dataset.
#    fitted() gives the predicted values; resid() gives the
#      residuals.
# CHANGE THIS: your dataset name before each $, and your model
#              name inside fitted() and resid()
students$predicted <- fitted(foot_model)
students$residual <- resid(foot_model)

The residual plot puts the predicted values across and the residuals up and down. Use it for the textbook’s linearity and equal variance checks:

# RESIDUAL PLOT: predicted values across, residuals up and down.
#    geom_hline(yintercept = 0) draws a horizontal line at 0
#      (no error). linetype = "dashed" makes it a dashed line.
ggplot(students, aes(x = predicted, y = residual)) +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Residual Plot",
       x = "Predicted foot length (cm)",
       y = "Residual (cm)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)




Residual plot for the foot length model.




Here the dots form an even band around the dashed line: no curve, and no megaphone shape. The slanted stripes come from foot lengths recorded to the nearest half centimeter, not from a problem with the model.
For the normality check, draw a histogram of the residuals, the same way you drew histograms in Chapter 1:

# HISTOGRAM OF THE RESIDUALS, to check that they form a rough
# bell curve. This is the histogram from Chapter 1.
ggplot(students, aes(x = residual)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "#0072B2", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Histogram of the Residuals",
       x = "Residual (cm)",
       y = "Number of students") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)




Histogram of the residuals from the foot length model.




The residuals form a rough bell curve centered at 0, which passes the check.






WarningCommon error: replacement has fewer rows than data



If your response or predictor has blank cells, lm() leaves those rows out, so the model has fewer residuals than the dataset has rows, and storing them as a new column stops with an error like this one (shown with Armspan, which has 34 blank cells):

armspan_model <- lm(Armspan ~ Height, data = students)
students$arm_residual <- resid(armspan_model)

Error in `$<-.data.frame`:
! replacement has 466 rows, data has 500


How to fix it: add na.action = na.exclude inside lm(). The model is the same, but fitted() and resid() then put a blank in each row that was left out, so the columns line up:

armspan_model <- lm(Armspan ~ Height, data = students,
                    na.action = na.exclude)
students$arm_residual <- resid(armspan_model)









TipWith your own data



Change the dataset name before each $ and the model name inside fitted() and resid(), then the labels on both graphs. In the histogram, choose a binwidth that suits your residuals’ units.
crumbs: 4  Correlation and Simple Linear Regression

title: 4  Correlation and Simple Linear Regression
text:
4.7 Influential points: Cook’s distance
Cook’s distance measures how much each point moves the regression line. A common rule of thumb treats a value above 1 as highly influential.

# 5. COOK'S DISTANCE: one value for each row.
#    max() shows the largest one.
#    which(... > 1) lists the rows above 1, the common cutoff.
# CHANGE THIS: your model name inside cooks.distance()
cooks <- cooks.distance(foot_model)
max(cooks)

[1] 0.03182956

which(cooks > 1)

named integer(0)


The largest Cook’s distance is 0.03, far below 1. named integer(0) means no rows are above 1, so no single student is pulling the line.






TipWith your own data



Change the model name. If which() lists rows, the numbers are row numbers in your dataset. To see those rows, put the numbers in square brackets, for example students[c(12, 40), ].
crumbs: 4  Correlation and Simple Linear Regression

title: 4  Correlation and Simple Linear Regression
text:
4.8 Confidence interval for the slope

# 6. 95% CONFIDENCE INTERVAL for the intercept and the slope.
# CHANGE THIS: your model name
confint(foot_model)

                 2.5 %      97.5 %
(Intercept) -5.7411458 -0.09286786
Height       0.1464325  0.17940499


Read the slope’s row (Height): we are 95% confident that, in the population, each extra centimeter of height goes with a foot between 0.146 and 0.179 centimeters longer, on average. The columns 2.5 % and 97.5 % are the two ends of a 95% interval.
crumbs: 4  Correlation and Simple Linear Regression

title: 4  Correlation and Simple Linear Regression
text:
4.9 Predictions
To predict from the model, set up the predictor value in a small dataset, then ask predict() for one of the two intervals the textbook describes:

# 7. PREDICTION for a new predictor value.
#    data.frame(Height = 170) sets up the value to predict from.
#      The name (Height) must match the predictor in the model.
#    interval = "confidence" gives the interval for the MEAN of
#      everyone with that height.
#    interval = "prediction" gives the interval for ONE person.
# CHANGE THIS: your predictor's name and the value you want, and
#              your model name
new_student <- data.frame(Height = 170)
predict(foot_model, new_student, interval = "confidence")

       fit      lwr      upr
1 24.77918 24.61066 24.94771

predict(foot_model, new_student, interval = "prediction")

       fit     lwr      upr
1 24.77918 21.0252 28.53317


For students 170 cm tall, the predicted foot length is 24.78 cm (fit). The confidence interval for the mean foot length of all such students is [24.61, 24.95]. The prediction interval for one such student is much wider, [21.03, 28.53], because individuals vary more than averages do. lwr and upr are the lower and upper ends.






WarningCommon error: object ‘Height’ not found



What you see

new_student <- data.frame(height = 170)
predict(foot_model, new_student, interval = "confidence")

Error:
! object 'Height' not found


What it means: the name inside data.frame() has to match the predictor’s name in the model exactly. Here it is height instead of Height.
How to fix it: copy the predictor’s name from your lm() line.








TipWith your own data



Change the predictor’s name and value inside data.frame(), and the model name. Predict only within the range of predictor values in your data; the textbook explains why predictions outside that range are risky.
crumbs: 4  Correlation and Simple Linear Regression

title: 4  Correlation and Simple Linear Regression
text:
4.10 Log transformation
When a scatterplot curves, a log transformation of the predictor can straighten it. Load the second dataset and draw the original scatterplot:

# 8. LOG TRANSFORMATION, with a second dataset.
# CHANGE THIS: the file name of your dataset, inside the quotes.
planet <- read.csv("happy_planet_index_2024.csv")


# First, the scatterplot on the original scale.
ggplot(planet, aes(x = Footprint, y = LifeExpectancy)) +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2") +
  labs(title = "Life Expectancy and Ecological Footprint",
       x = "Ecological footprint",
       y = "Life expectancy (years)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)




Scatterplot of life expectancy against ecological footprint for 147 countries.




The dots climb steeply and then level off, a curve of diminishing returns. Plot the base-10 log of the predictor instead by putting log10() around it:

# log10() takes the base-10 logarithm of each value. Putting it
# inside aes() plots the transformed values; the data stay as
# they are.
# CHANGE THIS: your predictor inside log10(), and your response
ggplot(planet, aes(x = log10(Footprint), y = LifeExpectancy)) +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Life Expectancy and Log of Footprint",
       x = "Ecological footprint (log base 10)",
       y = "Life expectancy (years)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'





Scatterplot of life expectancy against the base-10 log of ecological footprint, with the regression line.




The curve is gone. Fit the model the same way, with log10() around the predictor:

# The model works the same way, with log10() around the predictor.
# CHANGE THIS: your response, your predictor inside log10(), and
#              your dataset
log_model <- lm(LifeExpectancy ~ log10(Footprint), data = planet)
summary(log_model)


Call:
lm(formula = LifeExpectancy ~ log10(Footprint), data = planet)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-18.2244  -2.6984   0.8109   4.0421  11.5524 

Coefficients:
                 Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)       62.8086     0.8537   73.58   <2e-16 ***
log10(Footprint)  13.3925     1.0579   12.66   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 5.481 on 145 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.525, Adjusted R-squared:  0.5217 
F-statistic: 160.3 on 1 and 145 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


\(R^2\) is 0.525, or 52.5%, compared with 35.6% for a straight line on the original scale (the square of their correlation, 0.60). The slope, 13.39, is read as the textbook describes for a base-10 log: each time a country’s footprint multiplies by 10, predicted life expectancy rises by about 13.4 years.






WarningCommon error: NaNs produced



What you see

log10(c(10, 1, 0, -5))

Warning: NaNs produced


[1]    1    0 -Inf  NaN


What it means: the logarithm only exists for numbers above 0. log10(0) is -Inf (minus infinity) and the log of a negative number is NaN (“not a number”), so lm() cannot use those rows.
How to fix it: a log transformation only works for a predictor whose values are all above 0. If yours includes 0 or negative values, the textbook’s log transformation is not the right tool for that variable.








TipWith your own data



Put your predictor inside log10() in both the scatterplot and the model, and change the response and dataset. Interpret the slope as the change in the response each time the predictor multiplies by 10.

title: 5  Multiple Regression
text:
5.1 The data
This chapter builds the multiple regression models from Chapter 5 of the textbook: several numerical predictors, a binary predictor, a categorical predictor with three or more groups, and an interaction. It also checks for multicollinearity with VIF. Everything you learned about lm() and summary() in Chapter 4 still applies; a multiple regression just has more predictors after the ~.

Download acs_2023.csv into the same folder as the script. It holds 2023 American Community Survey answers from 10,000 U.S. adults.
The variables used in this chapter:

section: 5.2 Load the package and the data
text:
5.2 Load the package and the data
This chapter uses the car package for VIF. If you have not installed it yet, go back to Install and load packages in Getting Set Up.

# Load car, the package that calculates VIF.
library(car)

Loading required package: carData








NoteMessage: Loading required package: carData



car loads a companion package of example datasets when it starts. This message is normal.


Many people in the survey did not work last year, so they have 0 hours and no wages. The examples keep only the people who worked, using subset() from Chapter 3:

# CHANGE THIS: the file name of your dataset, inside the quotes.
census <- read.csv("acs_2023.csv")

# Keep only the people who worked at least one hour a week, using
# subset() from Chapter 3.
workers <- subset(census, HoursWk > 0)
nrow(workers)

[1] 5862


That leaves 5,862 workers.

title: 5  Multiple Regression
text:
5.3 Two numerical predictors
List the predictors after the ~, joined with + signs:

# 1. MULTIPLE REGRESSION: list the predictors after the ~,
#    joined with + signs.
#    Income ~ HoursWk + Age reads "Income, predicted by HoursWk and
#    Age".
# CHANGE THIS: your response, your predictors, your dataset, and a
#              name for your model
hours_model <- lm(Income ~ HoursWk + Age, data = workers)
summary(hours_model)


Call:
lm(formula = Income ~ HoursWk + Age, data = workers)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-161.99  -30.97  -12.56   10.40  719.57 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -36.07175    3.48616  -10.35   <2e-16 ***
HoursWk       1.71322    0.06901   24.82   <2e-16 ***
Age           0.66171    0.05828   11.35   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 70.61 on 5859 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1213,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.121 
F-statistic: 404.4 on 2 and 5859 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


The output has the same layout as in Chapter 4, with one row per predictor. Read it in the order the textbook does:

Is the model useful at all? The last line gives the F-statistic and its p-value for the whole model: \(F(2, 5859) = 404.4\), p < .001.
How much does it explain? Use Adjusted R-squared, not Multiple R-squared, for a multiple regression: 0.121, or 12.1% of the variation in income.
What does each predictor do? Read its Estimate while the others are held constant. Each extra hour worked per week goes with 1.71 more in income (in thousands, so about $1,710 a year), for workers of the same age.
Which predictor gives the stronger signal? Compare the t value column, not the slopes, because the predictors use different units. Hours worked (\(t = 24.82\)) gives a stronger signal than age (\(t = 11.35\)).







TipWith your own data



Change the response, the predictors, the dataset, and the model’s name. You can list as many predictors as you need, each joined with +.

title: 5  Multiple Regression
text:
5.4 A binary predictor
A predictor with two groups goes into the model like any other. Sex is coded 1 = male and 0 = female, so female is the baseline group and the slope is the difference for men:

# 2. BINARY PREDICTOR: a variable with two groups goes in the
#    model like any other predictor. Here Sex is coded 1 = male,
#    0 = female, so female is the baseline group.
# CHANGE THIS: add your binary predictor after another + sign
sex_model <- lm(Income ~ HoursWk + Age + Sex, data = workers)
summary(sex_model)

lm(formula = Income ~ HoursWk + Age + Sex, data = workers)

Residuals:

-162.70  -31.08  -12.41   10.81  714.05 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -38.91354    3.52223 -11.048  < 2e-16 ***
HoursWk       1.64976    0.06996  23.582  < 2e-16 ***
Age           0.66666    0.05816  11.462  < 2e-16 ***
Sex           9.62087    1.87087   5.142  2.8e-07 ***

title: 5  Multiple Regression
text:
5.6 Multicollinearity: VIF
vif(), from the car package, gives one variance inflation factor for each predictor:

# 4. VARIANCE INFLATION FACTORS: one VIF for each predictor.
#    vif() comes from the car package.
# CHANGE THIS: your model name
vif(sex_model)

 HoursWk      Age      Sex 
1.042313 1.010155 1.032119 


All three VIFs are close to 1, far below the usual danger zone of 5 (above 5, predictors overlap so much that the model cannot tell which one deserves the credit), so the predictors do not overlap enough to cause problems.






WarningCommon error: model contains fewer than 2 terms



What you see

one_predictor <- lm(Income ~ Age, data = workers)
vif(one_predictor)

Error in `vif.default()`:
! model contains fewer than 2 terms


What it means: VIF measures overlap between predictors, so it needs a model with at least two.
How to fix it: run vif() on a model with two or more predictors.








NoteGVIF for categorical predictors



If your model includes a categorical predictor with three or more groups, vif() prints a table headed GVIF instead, with one row per variable. Read the GVIF column the same way, with the same cutoff of 5.








TipWith your own data



Change the model name inside vif().

title: 5  Multiple Regression
text:
5.7 Interactions
An interaction asks whether the effect of one predictor depends on another. Joining two predictors with * puts both of them in the model and their interaction:

# 5. INTERACTION: a * between two predictors includes both of them
#    AND their interaction. Here the question is whether the
#    income difference for married people is the same for men and
#    women. Married is coded 1 = married, 0 = not married.
# CHANGE THIS: your two predictors, joined with *
interaction_model <- lm(Income ~ HoursWk + Age + Sex * Married,
                        data = workers)
summary(interaction_model)


Call:
lm(formula = Income ~ HoursWk + Age + Sex * Married, data = workers)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-153.14  -30.30  -10.37   10.70  715.42 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -28.49994    3.65592  -7.796 7.54e-15 ***
HoursWk       1.52453    0.06958  21.911  < 2e-16 ***
Age           0.36828    0.06187   5.953 2.79e-09 ***
Sex          -0.97253    2.57758  -0.377    0.706    
Married      13.51728    2.69781   5.010 5.59e-07 ***
Sex:Married  20.83521    3.63800   5.727 1.07e-08 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 69.41 on 5856 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1513,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.1505 
F-statistic: 208.7 on 5 and 5856 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


The interaction row is named after both variables, joined with a colon: Sex:Married. Read it in three steps:

Check the interaction’s p-value first. Here it is \(1.07 \times 10^{-8}\) (printed 1.07e-08), well below .05, so the interaction is significant and stays in the model.
Ignore the p-values of Sex and Married on their own, because they no longer test a general effect. Keep both variables in the model anyway (the hierarchy rule); the * does this for you.
Read the slopes as switches. For women (Sex = 0), being married goes with 13.52 more in income (about $13,520). For men (Sex = 1), add the interaction too: \(13.52 + 20.84 = 34.36\), about $34,360. The income difference for married people is much larger for men than for women.

If the interaction had not been significant, you would remove it (write Sex + Married instead of Sex * Married), fit the model again, and then read the p-values for the individual variables.






TipWith your own data



Join the two predictors you think interact with *, and keep any other predictors joined with +. Find the row whose name has a colon, and check its p-value before anything else.

title: 6  The One-Way ANOVA
text:
6.1 The data
This chapter follows the one-way ANOVA from Chapter 6 of the textbook from start to finish: check the equal variances and normality assumptions, run the global ANOVA, then find which groups differ with Tukey’s HSD or Dunnett’s test and measure the size of a difference with Cohen’s d.
Get the script: Download the Chapter 6 script, chapter_06.R, and save it in the same folder as your data.
Download smoking_bmi_bp.csv into the same folder as the script. It holds blood pressure readings for 500 randomly selected U.S. adults. The question in this chapter: does systolic blood pressure differ across BMI categories?
The variables used in this chapter:
