6.2 Load the packages and the data
This chapter uses three packages: ggplot2 for the graphs, emmeans for Dunnett’s test, and effectsize for Cohen’s d. If any is not installed yet, go back to Install and load packages in Getting Set Up.

# ggplot2 draws the graphs, emmeans runs Dunnett's test, and
# effectsize calculates Cohen's d.
library(ggplot2)
library(emmeans)

Welcome to emmeans.
Caution: You lose important information if you filter this package's results.
See '? untidy'

library(effectsize)







NoteMessage: Welcome to emmeans



emmeans prints a welcome note when it loads. The message is normal, and you can ignore it.



# CHANGE THIS: the file name of your dataset, inside the quotes.
pressure <- read.csv("smoking_bmi_bp.csv")
names(pressure)

[1] "SystolicBP" "Smoker"     "BMI"       








NoteColumns named X, X.1, X.2, and so on



This file has six empty columns after the real ones, and R names them X through X.5. Files saved from spreadsheet programs often pick up empty columns like these. They hold nothing, and you can ignore them.

title: 6  The One-Way ANOVA
text:
6.3 Put the groups in order
R lists groups in alphabetical order unless you tell it otherwise, which here would put Obese before Overweight. factor() with levels = sets the order used in every table and graph that follows:

# Put the groups in a sensible order. Without this, R uses
# alphabetical order (Normal, Obese, Overweight).
#    factor(..., levels = c(...)) lists the groups in the order
#    you want, spelled exactly as in the data.
# CHANGE THIS: your group variable (in both places) and your
#              groups, in order
pressure$BMI <- factor(pressure$BMI,
                       levels = c("Normal", "Overweight", "Obese"))







WarningCommon error: a group turns into NA



What you see

misspelled <- factor(c("Normal", "Overweight", "Obese"),
                     levels = c("Normal", "overweight", "Obese"))
misspelled

[1] Normal <NA>   Obese 
Levels: Normal overweight Obese


What it means: any value not listed in levels = exactly as it is spelled in the data becomes NA. Here overweight is lowercase, so every Overweight person would drop out of the analysis.
How to fix it: copy each group name exactly from table() of your variable, and check the result with table() again afterward.

title: 6  The One-Way ANOVA
text:
6.4 Check equal variances
Check equal variances with a rule of thumb and a picture: the 2X rule and a jitter plot. You may see formal tests for equal variances elsewhere; they tend to be overly sensitive, and using a hypothesis test to decide whether you may run a hypothesis test goes in a circle. Start with each group’s mean and standard deviation:

# 1. GROUP MEANS AND STANDARD DEVIATIONS, with tapply() from
#    Chapter 3. The standard deviations are stored as group_sds
#    so the next line can use them.
# CHANGE THIS: your numerical variable and your group variable
tapply(pressure$SystolicBP, pressure$BMI, mean)

    Normal Overweight      Obese 
  136.3155   144.3670   153.1814 

group_sds <- tapply(pressure$SystolicBP, pressure$BMI, sd)
group_sds

    Normal Overweight      Obese 
  27.26852   25.07864   27.81397 

# THE 2X RULE: the largest standard deviation divided by the
# smallest. A result of 2 or less passes the check.
max(group_sds) / min(group_sds)

[1] 1.10907


The largest standard deviation is only 1.11 times the smallest, well under 2, so the groups pass the 2X rule. (The means, 136.3, 144.4, and 153.2 mmHg, are what you report for each group.)
Then draw the jitter plot, with a black diamond at each group’s mean:

# 2. JITTER PLOT: one dot per person, nudged sideways so the dots
#    do not pile up.
#    geom_jitter(width = 0.2) spreads the dots 0.2 of a group's
#      width to each side. height = 0 keeps their values exact.
#    alpha = 0.5 makes the dots see-through, so overlaps show.
#    stat_summary(fun = mean, ...) adds each group's mean.
#      shape = 18 is a diamond; size = 5 makes it large.
# set.seed() fixes the random sideways nudges, so the plot looks
# the same every time you run it. Any whole number works.
set.seed(2026)

# CHANGE THIS: your group variable after x =, your numerical
#              variable after y =, and your labels
ggplot(pressure, aes(x = BMI, y = SystolicBP)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0, alpha = 0.5,
              color = "#0072B2") +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 18, size = 5,
               color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Systolic Blood Pressure by BMI Category",
       x = "BMI category",
       y = "Systolic blood pressure (mmHg)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)




Jitter plot of systolic blood pressure by BMI category, with group means marked by diamonds.




The dots spread about the same distance from top to bottom in all three groups, which supports the equal variances assumption.






TipWith your own data



Change the numerical variable and the group variable in the tapply() lines and the plot, and update the labels. set.seed() only makes the random sideways nudges repeatable; you can keep any number there.

title: 6  The One-Way ANOVA
text:
6.5 The global ANOVA
aov() (short for “analysis of variance”) is written like lm(): the numerical variable before the ~, the group variable after it.

# 3. ONE-WAY ANOVA: aov() is written like lm(), with the
#    numerical variable before the ~ and the group variable after.
# CHANGE THIS: your numerical variable, your group variable, your
#              dataset, and a name for your model
bp_model <- aov(SystolicBP ~ BMI, data = pressure)
summary(bp_model)

             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value  Pr(>F)    
BMI           2  27801   13900   19.02 1.1e-08 ***
Residuals   497 363274     731                    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The BMI row holds the values to report:

Where each value appears in the ANOVA table







What you report
Where it is in the output
In this example




Between-groups degrees of freedom
BMI row, Df column
2


Within-groups degrees of freedom
Residuals row, Df column
497


\(F\) statistic
BMI row, F value column
19.02


p-value
BMI row, Pr(>F) column
below .001 (1.1e-08)



So \(F(2, 497) = 19.02\), p < .001: at least one BMI category has a different mean systolic blood pressure. As the textbook stresses, this does not say which ones; that is the job of the post hoc tests below.






NoteCheck: Df of 1 for the groups



If the group variable’s row shows Df of 1 when you have three or more groups, R treated your groups as a number. This happens when groups are stored as codes such as 1, 2, and 3. Wrap the variable in factor() (as in Put the groups in order) and run aov() again. The between-groups degrees of freedom should be the number of groups minus 1.

title: 6  The One-Way ANOVA
text:
6.6 Check normality: Q-Q plot
Store the model’s residuals as a new column, as in Chapter 4, and draw a normal Q-Q plot:

# 4. NORMAL Q-Q PLOT of the residuals.
#    Store the residuals as a new column, as in Chapter 4.
#    aes(sample = residual) tells ggplot which values to check.
#    stat_qq() draws the dots; stat_qq_line() draws the
#      reference line.
# CHANGE THIS: your dataset name and your model name
pressure$residual <- resid(bp_model)

ggplot(pressure, aes(sample = residual)) +
  stat_qq(color = "#0072B2") +
  stat_qq_line() +
  labs(title = "Normal Q-Q Plot of the Residuals",
       x = "Expected if normal (theoretical quantiles)",
       y = "Residuals (sample quantiles)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)




Normal Q-Q plot of the ANOVA residuals.




The dots follow the reference line closely, bending only slightly at the ends, so the residuals are reasonably normal. What would fail this check, as the textbook describes, is dots that pull sharply away from the line in a hook at one or both ends.






TipWith your own data



Change the dataset name and the model name in the first line. The plot code itself does not change.

title: 6  The One-Way ANOVA
text:
6.7 Tukey’s HSD
Tukey’s HSD compares every pair of groups and adjusts the p-values for the number of comparisons:

# 5. TUKEY'S HSD: compares every pair of groups.
# CHANGE THIS: your model name
TukeyHSD(bp_model)

  Tukey multiple comparisons of means
    95% family-wise confidence level

Fit: aov(formula = SystolicBP ~ BMI, data = pressure)

$BMI
                       diff        lwr      upr     p adj
Overweight-Normal  8.051464  0.3927115 15.71022 0.0366867
Obese-Normal      16.865865 10.4316024 23.30013 0.0000000
Obese-Overweight   8.814400  1.2740746 16.35473 0.0170703


Each row is one pair. diff is the difference in means (the first group named minus the second), lwr and upr are the ends of its 95% confidence interval, and p adj is the adjusted p-value. All three pairs differ significantly. For example, the Obese group’s mean is 16.87 mmHg higher than the Normal group’s, 95% CI [10.43, 23.30].






NoteA p adj of 0.0000000



R rounds the p-value to seven decimal places, so 0.0000000 means it is smaller than 0.00000005, not exactly zero. Report it as p < .001.

title: 6  The One-Way ANOVA
text:
6.8 Dunnett’s test
When one group is a control (here, Normal BMI), Dunnett’s test compares each other group to it and skips the rest. It comes from the emmeans package:

# 6. DUNNETT'S test: compares each group only to the control.
#    emmeans(model, "BMI") calculates each group's mean from the
#      model. The name in quotes is your group variable.
#    method = "trt.vs.ctrl" means "each treatment versus the
#      control".
#    ref = 1 makes the first group in your order (here, Normal)
#      the control.
# CHANGE THIS: your model name and your group variable; set the
#              order of your groups so the control comes first
group_means <- emmeans(bp_model, "BMI")
dunnett <- contrast(group_means, method = "trt.vs.ctrl", ref = 1)
dunnett

 contrast            estimate   SE  df t.ratio p.value
 Overweight - Normal     8.05 3.26 497   2.471  0.0266
 Obese - Normal         16.87 2.74 497   6.162 <0.0001

P value adjustment: dunnettx method for 2 tests 

confint(dunnett)

 contrast            estimate   SE  df lower.CL upper.CL
 Overweight - Normal     8.05 3.26 497    0.792     15.3
 Obese - Normal         16.87 2.74 497   10.767     23.0

Confidence level used: 0.95 
Conf-level adjustment: dunnettx method for 2 estimates 


The first table gives the differences and p-values; confint() adds their 95% confidence intervals. Both groups have significantly higher blood pressure than the Normal group: Overweight by 8.05 mmHg (p = .027) and Obese by 16.87 mmHg (p < .001).






TipWith your own data



Change the model name and the group variable inside emmeans(). ref = 1 means the first group in your order is the control, so put your control group first when you set the order with factor().

title: 6  The One-Way ANOVA
section: 6.9 Cohen’s d for a pair of groups
text:
6.9 Cohen’s d for a pair of groups
For practical significance, calculate Cohen’s d for a pair the post hoc test found significant. Keep just those two groups with subset() and %in%, then use cohens_d() from Chapter 3:

# 7. COHEN'S d for one pair of groups, as in Chapter 3.
#    %in% c(...) keeps the rows whose group is one of the two
#      named, so the test sees only that pair.
# CHANGE THIS: your variables, your dataset, and the two groups
cohens_d(SystolicBP ~ BMI,
         data = subset(pressure, BMI %in% c("Normal", "Obese")))

Cohen's d |         95% CI
--------------------------
-0.61     | [-0.81, -0.41]

- Estimated using pooled SD.


The difference between the Normal and Obese groups is \(d = 0.61\) (ignore the minus sign, which only reflects the order of the groups): a medium effect.






TipWith your own data



Change the variables, the dataset, and the two group names inside c(). Repeat the line once for each pair you need.

NoteMessages: carData and Welcome to emmeans



Both packages print a message when they load: car loads a companion package of example datasets, and emmeans prints a welcome note. Both messages are normal, and you can ignore them.


The options(contrasts = ...) line changes a setting so that R calculates main effects with Type III sums of squares, which test each factor after accounting for everything else in the model, so the result does not depend on the order you list the factors. You never need to change it.






NoteCheck: main effects that do not match



If you skip the options(contrasts = ...) line, Anova(..., type = 3) still prints a table with no error or warning, but the main effect rows of a model with an interaction test something different. Your numbers will not match this chapter or the textbook. If your main effects look different from what you expect, check that you ran this line before fitting the model, then fit the model again.

title: 7  Two-Way ANOVA, ANCOVA, and Repeated Measures
text:
7.3 Two-way ANOVA
The question: does systolic blood pressure depend on BMI category, on smoking, or on the combination of the two?

# CHANGE THIS: the file name of your dataset, inside the quotes.
pressure <- read.csv("smoking_bmi_bp.csv")

# Put the BMI groups in order, as in Chapter 6.
pressure$BMI <- factor(pressure$BMI,
                       levels = c("Normal", "Overweight", "Obese"))


7.3.1 Check the cells
Check a two-way ANOVA’s assumptions at the level of the cells, the subgroups formed by crossing the two factors (here, 3 BMI groups × 2 smoking groups = 6 cells), because the model treats each cell as its own group. Putting both factors inside list() makes tapply() calculate one value per cell:

# 1. TWO-WAY ANOVA.
#    Cell means and standard deviations. Inside tapply(),
#    list(first, second) splits the data by BOTH factors at once,
#    giving one value per cell.
# CHANGE THIS: your numerical variable and your two factors
tapply(pressure$SystolicBP,
       list(pressure$BMI, pressure$Smoker), mean)

                 No      Yes
Normal     130.3814 142.7111
Overweight 140.7458 148.6400
Obese      148.9487 155.8016

cell_sds <- tapply(pressure$SystolicBP,
                   list(pressure$BMI, pressure$Smoker), sd)
cell_sds

                 No      Yes
Normal     28.91454 23.92556
Overweight 23.09993 26.83644
Obese      25.44814 28.97116

# The 2X rule, across all the cells.
max(cell_sds) / min(cell_sds)

[1] 1.254167


The largest cell standard deviation is 1.25 times the smallest, under 2, so the cells pass the 2X rule. For the normality check, draw a Q-Q plot of the model’s residuals with the code from Chapter 6, after fitting the model below.


7.3.2 Interaction plot
An interaction plot draws one line per group of the second factor, joining the cell means:

# INTERACTION PLOT: one line per Smoker group, joining the group
# means across the BMI categories.
#    color =, linetype =, and shape = all show the Smoker group,
#      so the lines can be told apart without color.
#    stat_summary(fun = mean, ...) plots the mean, drawn as a line
#      and as points.
# CHANGE THIS: your first factor after x =, your numerical
#              variable after y =, and your second factor in the
#              four places it appears
ggplot(pressure, aes(x = BMI, y = SystolicBP, color = Smoker,
                     linetype = Smoker, shape = Smoker,
                     group = Smoker)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line", linewidth = 1) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00")) +
  labs(title = "Mean Systolic Blood Pressure",
       x = "BMI category",
       y = "Mean systolic blood pressure (mmHg)",
       color = "Smoker", linetype = "Smoker", shape = "Smoker") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)




Interaction plot of mean systolic blood pressure by BMI category, with one line for smokers and one for nonsmokers.




The smokers’ line sits above the nonsmokers’ line in every BMI category, and the two lines are close to parallel. Parallel lines suggest no interaction; the ANOVA tells you whether any gap between them is more than noise.


7.3.3 The ANOVA table
Fit the model with lm() and both factors joined by *, then print the table with Anova() from the car package:

# THE TWO-WAY ANOVA.
#    BMI * Smoker includes both factors and their interaction,
#      as in Chapter 5.
#    Anova(..., type = 3) from the car package prints the Type III
#      table.
# CHANGE THIS: your numerical variable, your two factors, your
#              dataset, and a name for your model
pressure_model <- lm(SystolicBP ~ BMI * Smoker, data = pressure)
Anova(pressure_model, type = 3)

Anova Table (Type III tests)

Response: SystolicBP
             Sum Sq  Df    F value    Pr(>F)    
(Intercept) 9504842   1 13330.5504 < 2.2e-16 ***
BMI           23763   2    16.6637 9.925e-08 ***
Smoker         9266   1    12.9950  0.000344 ***
BMI:Smoker      769   2     0.5391  0.583614    
Residuals    352228 494                         
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Ignore the (Intercept) row. Then follow the stop sign rule:

The interaction first. The BMI:Smoker row has p = .584, far above .05. The interaction is not significant, so the stop sign turns green.
Then the main effects. BMI category has a significant main effect, \(F(2, 494) = 16.66\), p < .001, and so does smoking, \(F(1, 494) = 12.99\), p < .001. Each row’s Df is its first degrees of freedom, and the Residuals row’s Df (494) is the second.

If the interaction had been significant, you would stop at step 1 and describe the interaction (using the plot) instead of the main effects.






TipWith your own data



Change the numerical variable and the two factors everywhere they appear: in tapply(), the plot (the second factor appears four times inside aes()), and the model. If a factor’s groups are stored as numbers, wrap it in factor() first, as in Chapter 6.

title: 7  Two-Way ANOVA, ANCOVA, and Repeated Measures
text:
7.4 ANCOVA
The question: do female and male students differ in foot length once height is taken into account? Height is the covariate, the numerical variable the ANCOVA levels the playing field on.

# CHANGE THIS: the file name of your dataset, inside the quotes.
students <- read.csv("census_at_school.csv")


7.4.1 Check the slopes
The key ANCOVA assumption is that the covariate relates to the response the same way in every group, so that one adjustment is fair to all of them. Test it with the covariate-by-group interaction:

# 2. ANCOVA.
#    First, the assumption check: does the covariate (Height)
#    relate to the response (Foot) the same way in each group?
#    Height * Gender tests the covariate-by-group interaction.
# CHANGE THIS: your response, your covariate, your group
#              variable, and your dataset
slopes_check <- lm(Foot ~ Height * Gender, data = students)
Anova(slopes_check, type = 3)

Anova Table (Type III tests)

Response: Foot
               Sum Sq  Df  F value  Pr(>F)    
(Intercept)     14.96   1   4.3551 0.03741 *  
Height         379.14   1 110.3500 < 2e-16 ***
Gender           3.87   1   1.1263 0.28908    
Height:Gender    6.59   1   1.9178 0.16672    
Residuals     1704.17 496                     
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The Height:Gender row has p = .167, above .05, so the slopes are similar enough and the ANCOVA can go ahead. (If this interaction were significant, the groups’ slopes would differ, and an ANCOVA would not be appropriate.)
The other new assumption, linearity, is checked with a scatterplot of the response against the covariate, using the code from Chapter 4.


7.4.2 The ANCOVA table
The ANCOVA itself uses + instead of *, leaving the interaction out:

# THE ANCOVA: the covariate and the group, joined with + (no
# interaction).
# CHANGE THIS: the same variables, joined with +
foot_model <- lm(Foot ~ Height + Gender, data = students)
Anova(foot_model, type = 3)

Anova Table (Type III tests)

Response: Foot
             Sum Sq  Df  F value    Pr(>F)    
(Intercept)   19.18   1   5.5715   0.01864 *  
Height       372.55   1 108.2324 < 2.2e-16 ***
Gender       103.63   1  30.1051  6.53e-08 ***
Residuals   1710.76 497                       
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1



The covariate row (Height): height strongly predicts foot length, \(F(1, 497) = 108.23\), p < .001.
The group row (Gender): female and male students differ in foot length even after accounting for height, \(F(1, 497) = 30.11\), p < .001.



7.4.3 Adjusted means
emmeans() gives each group’s adjusted mean: its predicted mean for students of the same, average height.

# ADJUSTED MEANS: each group's mean foot length for students of
# the same (average) height. The name in quotes is your group
# variable.
# CHANGE THIS: your model name and your group variable
emmeans(foot_model, "Gender")

 Gender emmean    SE  df lower.CL upper.CL
 Female   24.3 0.139 497     24.1     24.6
 Male     25.6 0.147 497     25.3     25.9

Confidence level used: 0.95 

# For comparison, the raw (unadjusted) group means.
tapply(students$Foot, students$Gender, mean)

  Female     Male 
23.51423 26.48917 


The raw means differ by almost 3 cm (23.51 vs. 26.49), but most of that gap comes from male students being taller on average. For students of the same height, the adjusted means differ by only about 1.3 cm (24.3 vs. 25.6). The lower.CL and upper.CL columns are each adjusted mean’s 95% confidence interval.






TipWith your own data



Change the response, covariate, group variable, and dataset in both models, and the model name and group variable in emmeans(). Use a covariate measured before the treatment or grouping could affect it (for example, a baseline score). If the treatment changed the covariate, adjusting for it would remove part of the effect you are trying to measure.

title: 7  Two-Way ANOVA, ANCOVA, and Repeated Measures
text:
7.5 Repeated measures ANOVA
The question: do students sleep a different amount on school nights and non-school nights, and is that difference the same for female and male students? Each student answered both sleep questions, so the two measurements are within-subjects, and Gender is the between-subjects factor.
The data are in wide form: one row per student, with the two measurements in separate columns. The repeated measures ANOVA takes three steps:

# 3. REPEATED MEASURES ANOVA, with the data in "wide" form: one
#    row per person, one column per time point.
#    cbind(Sleep1, Sleep2) joins the two measurements of the same
#      people, in time order. Gender is the between-subjects
#      factor.
# CHANGE THIS: your repeated measurements inside cbind(), your
#              between-subjects factor, and your dataset
sleep_model <- lm(cbind(Sleep1, Sleep2) ~ Gender, data = students)

#    nights names the measurements, in the same order as in
#      cbind(): a factor called Night with two levels.
# CHANGE THIS: a name for your time factor and a label for each
#              measurement, in order
nights <- data.frame(Night = factor(c("School", "Weekend")))

#    idata = nights and idesign = ~ Night tell Anova() which
#      columns are the repeated measurements.
#    multivariate = FALSE prints the standard ANOVA table.
# CHANGE THIS: your time factor's name after the ~
sleep_anova <- Anova(sleep_model, idata = nights,
                     idesign = ~ Night, type = 3)
summary(sleep_anova, multivariate = FALSE)


Univariate Type III Repeated-Measures ANOVA Assuming Sphericity

             Sum Sq num Df Error SS den Df    F value Pr(>F)    
(Intercept)   61371      1  1059.70    498 28840.8544 <2e-16 ***
Gender            0      1  1059.70    498     0.0169 0.8965    
Night          1089      1   721.24    498   752.1426 <2e-16 ***
Gender:Night      4      1   721.24    498     2.6174 0.1063    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1



cbind(Sleep1, Sleep2) joins the two measurements of the same students into the response, in time order.
nights names them: a factor called Night with one label per measurement, in the same order as cbind().
Anova() with idata and idesign uses those names to run the test. multivariate = FALSE prints the standard table (a longer multivariate version prints if you leave it out).

Read the table with the same stop sign rule, ignoring the (Intercept) row:

Reading the repeated measures table







Row
What it tests
In this example




Gender:Night
The interaction: does the change from school to non-school nights differ by gender?
\(F(1, 498) = 2.62\), p = .106, not significant


Night
The main effect of time
\(F(1, 498) = 752.14\), p < .001


Gender
The main effect of the between-subjects factor
\(F(1, 498) = 0.02\), p = .897



The interaction is not significant, so the main effects can be read: students sleep significantly more on non-school nights, and female and male students do not differ in their overall sleep. The degrees of freedom for each row are num Df and den Df.






WarningCommon error: the labels do not match the measurements



What you see

three_labels <- data.frame(Night = factor(c("School", "Weekend",
                                            "Holiday")))
Anova(sleep_model, idata = three_labels, idesign = ~ Night,
      type = 3)

Error in `dimnames(x) <- dn`:
! length of 'dimnames' [1] not equal to array extent


What it means: cbind() joined two measurements, but nights has three labels. The number of labels must match the number of measurements.
How to fix it: give the factor exactly one label per column inside cbind(), in the same order.








TipWith your own data



Put your repeated measurements inside cbind() in time order, and your between-subjects factor after the ~. Then give the time factor a name and one label per measurement, and use that name after idesign = ~. With three or more time points, list them all in cbind() and give one label each.

section: 8.2 Load the package and the data
text:
8.2 Load the package and the data
This chapter uses the effectsize package for Cramér’s V. If you have not installed it yet, go back to Install and load packages in Getting Set Up.

# effectsize calculates Cramer's V. Everything else in this
# chapter is built into R.
library(effectsize)


# CHANGE THIS: the file name of your dataset, inside the quotes.
students <- read.csv("census_at_school.csv")

title: 8  Categorical Data Analysis
text:
8.3 Goodness-of-fit test
The question: are all four seasons equally popular as students’ favorite? A goodness-of-fit test compares the counts in one categorical variable to a set of expected proportions. Count the categories with table(), then give chisq.test() the proportions you expect:

# 1. GOODNESS-OF-FIT: does one categorical variable match a set of
#    expected proportions?
#    table() counts each category, in alphabetical order.
# CHANGE THIS: your categorical variable
season_counts <- table(students$Season)
season_counts


  Fall Spring Summer Winter 
   182     65    179     74 

#    p = c(...) lists the expected proportion for each category,
#      as decimals, in the SAME order as the table above. They
#      must add up to 1. Here every season is expected to be
#      equally popular (0.25 each).
# CHANGE THIS: the table name and your expected proportions
season_test <- chisq.test(season_counts,
                          p = c(0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25))
season_test


    Chi-squared test for given probabilities

data:  season_counts
X-squared = 98.928, df = 3, p-value < 2.2e-16


The proportions after p = must be in the same order as the categories in the table, which R puts in alphabetical order (Fall, Spring, Summer, Winter). Here every season gets 0.25. With a published baseline, such as the Census proportions in the textbook, you would type those proportions instead.
The result: \(\chi^2(3, N = 500) = 98.93\), p < .001. The df in the output is the degrees of freedom, and N is the total of the counts. The seasons are not equally popular.






WarningCommon error: probabilities must sum to 1



What you see

chisq.test(season_counts, p = c(0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.20))

Error in `chisq.test()`:
! probabilities must sum to 1.


What it means: the proportions after p = add up to 0.95, not 1.
How to fix it: check your proportions and make sure they add up to exactly 1. If they come from a published source and only miss 1 because of rounding, add rescale.p = TRUE inside chisq.test(), as the textbook’s code does, and R scales them up to 1 for you.



8.3.1 Expected counts and standardized residuals
Two more pieces of the test’s results finish the analysis:

# The expected counts (check that each one is at least 5) and the
# standardized residuals, rounded to 2 decimal places.
#    $stdres holds the standardized residuals. Use $stdres, not
#      $residuals, which holds a different kind of residual.
# CHANGE THIS: your test's name, in both lines
season_test$expected

  Fall Spring Summer Winter 
   125    125    125    125 

round(season_test$stdres, 2)


  Fall Spring Summer Winter 
  5.89  -6.20   5.58  -5.27 



$expected gives the expected counts. Every one must be at least 5, the usual rule of thumb; below 5, the p-value is no longer trustworthy. Here each is 125.
$stdres gives the standardized residuals, which work like z-scores. A common rule of thumb flags any value outside \(-2\) to \(+2\). Fall (5.89) and Summer (5.58) are chosen more often than expected, and Spring (\(-6.20\)) and Winter (\(-5.27\)) less often.

The $ works here the same way it does for a dataset: it picks out one part of the test’s results by name.






WarningCheck: $stdres, not $residuals



The results also include $residuals, which R prints without any warning. These are a different kind of residual, and they come out smaller than the standardized residuals (here, Fall would be 5.10 instead of 5.89), so the \(\pm 2\) rule does not apply to them. Always use $stdres.








TipWith your own data



Change the variable inside table(), then list one expected proportion for each category in alphabetical order. Use table() first to see the order R uses, and count the categories so the list has one proportion per category.

title: 8  Categorical Data Analysis
text:
8.4 Test for independence
The question: are gender and desired superpower related? Build the cross-tabulation with table(), putting one variable in the rows and the other in the columns. Row proportions, from Chapter 2, make the rows easier to compare:

# 2. test FOR INDEPENDENCE: are two categorical variables related?
#    table(rows, columns) builds the cross-tabulation.
#    prop.table(..., margin = 1) turns each row into proportions,
#      as in Chapter 2, so the rows can be compared.
# CHANGE THIS: your two categorical variables
power_table <- table(students$Gender, students$Superpower)
power_table

        
         Fly Freeze time Invisibility Super strength Telepathy
  Female  69          62           49              4        76
  Male    51          81           33             31        44

round(prop.table(power_table, margin = 1), 2)

        
          Fly Freeze time Invisibility Super strength Telepathy
  Female 0.27        0.24         0.19           0.02      0.29
  Male   0.21        0.34         0.14           0.13      0.18

# The test. With a cross-tabulation, chisq.test() needs nothing
# else: it calculates the expected counts itself.
# CHANGE THIS: your table's name, and a name for the test
power_test <- chisq.test(power_table)
power_test


    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  power_table
X-squared = 36.967, df = 4, p-value = 1.829e-07


Super strength stands out: 13% of male students chose it, compared with 2% of female students. The test: \(\chi^2(4, N = 500) = 36.97\), p < .001, so gender and desired superpower are related.

# Expected counts and standardized residuals for every cell.
# round(..., 1) rounds to 1 decimal place.
# CHANGE THIS: your test's name, in both lines
round(power_test$expected, 1)

        
          Fly Freeze time Invisibility Super strength Telepathy
  Female 62.4        74.4         42.6           18.2      62.4
  Male   57.6        68.6         39.4           16.8      57.6

round(power_test$stdres, 2)

        
           Fly Freeze time Invisibility Super strength Telepathy
  Female  1.38       -2.45         1.54          -4.98      2.85
  Male   -1.38        2.45        -1.54           4.98     -2.85


Every expected count is at least 5 (the smallest is 16.8), so the assumption holds. Three columns have standardized residuals outside \(-2\) to \(+2\). Male students chose Super strength (4.98) and Freeze time (2.45) more often than expected, and Telepathy less often (\(-2.85\)); female students show the opposite pattern. Fly and Invisibility fall inside the range. With two rows, each cell’s residual is the exact opposite of the one below it, so reading one row is enough.






NoteThe test for homogeneity uses the same code



The textbook’s test for homogeneity differs from the test for independence in the study design (how the data were collected), not the calculations. In R, both use exactly the same table() and chisq.test() lines. Put the populations you are comparing in the rows.








WarningCommon error: Chi-squared approximation may be incorrect



What you see

chisq.test(table(students$Gender, students$GetToSchool))

Warning in chisq.test(table(students$Gender,
students$GetToSchool)): Chi-squared approximation may be incorrect



    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  table(students$Gender, students$GetToSchool)
X-squared = 6.0828, df = 2, p-value = 0.04777


What it means: this is a warning, not an error, so R still prints a result. It means at least one expected count is below 5 (here, very few students walk to school), so the p-value cannot be trusted. Check with $expected to see which cells are too small.
How to fix it: do not report this p-value. You have two options: combine small categories into larger, meaningful ones (as the textbook does with the armed variable), or use Fisher’s Exact Test from Chapter 10, which has no minimum expected count.



8.4.1 Cramér’s V
cramers_v() measures the strength of the relationship:

# CRAMER'S V, from the effectsize package.
#    adjust = FALSE gives the standard Cramer's V, the version the
#    cutoffs in the textbook's Table 8.3 are for. (Leaving it out
#    gives a slightly smaller, bias-adjusted version.)
# CHANGE THIS: your table's name
cramers_v(power_table, adjust = FALSE)

Cramer's V |       95% CI
-------------------------
0.27       | [0.18, 1.00]

- One-sided CIs: upper bound fixed at [1.00].


\(V = 0.27\). Cramér’s V cutoffs depend on the size of the table, because more categories spread the data out. Find the row for the number of categories in the smaller variable:

The 95% CI is a range of likely values; its upper end is always printed as 1.00, and the note under the table says so. You can ignore it.






TipWith your own data



Put your two categorical variables inside table(), then change the table name in chisq.test() and cramers_v(). Count the categories in each variable, and use the smaller count to pick the row of the cutoff table above. For a 2 × 2 table, the same function gives Phi.

title: 8  Categorical Data Analysis
text:
8.5 McNemar’s test
McNemar’s test is for paired yes/no answers: the same people, two times or two questions. The question here: is the share of students who sleep at least 8 hours different on school nights and non-school nights?
The data hold hours of sleep, not yes/no answers, so the first two lines create the yes/no columns with ifelse(). If your data already have two yes/no columns, skip those lines.

# 3. McNEMAR'S test: the same people answer two yes/no questions.
#    Here the two "questions" are whether each student sleeps at
#    least 8 hours on a school night and on a non-school night.
#    ifelse(test, "Yes", "No") gives "Yes" for each row where the
#      test is true, and "No" where it is false.
# CHANGE THIS: your variables, your cutoff, and new column names.
#              (If your data already hold two yes/no columns,
#              skip these two lines.)
students$Enough1 <- ifelse(students$Sleep1 >= 8, "Yes", "No")
students$Enough2 <- ifelse(students$Sleep2 >= 8, "Yes", "No")

#    Inside table(), Name = column gives each side a label.
# CHANGE THIS: your labels and your two yes/no columns
sleep_table <- table(SchoolNight = students$Enough1,
                     NonSchoolNight = students$Enough2)
sleep_table

           NonSchoolNight
SchoolNight  No Yes
        No   53 332
        Yes  10 105

mcnemar.test(sleep_table)


    McNemar's Chi-squared test with continuity correction

data:  sleep_table
McNemar's chi-squared = 301.29, df = 1, p-value < 2.2e-16


The two disagreement cells are what the test compares: 332 students sleep 8 hours or more only on non-school nights, and 10 only on school nights. \(\chi^2(1, N = 500) = 301.29\), p < .001, so students are much more likely to reach 8 hours on non-school nights. As the textbook says, no post hoc test is needed: compare those two cells to see which way the difference goes.






NoteContinuity correction



The output’s title says “with continuity correction.” That is a small adjustment R makes by default for a 2 × 2 table, where the chi-square p-value otherwise comes out a little too small. It also matches the textbook’s results, so you do not need to change anything.








TipWith your own data



Put the two yes/no columns in table(), in the same order as they happened. The labels before each = are names for the table and can be anything.

title: 8  Categorical Data Analysis
section: 8.6 Relative risk and the odds ratio
text:
8.6 Relative risk and the odds ratio
The question: compared with citizens, how likely are noncitizens to have health insurance? Both variables are coded 0 and 1. Put the groups you are comparing in the rows and the outcome in the columns, then turn each row into proportions, the risk of each outcome:

# CHANGE THIS: the file name of your dataset, inside the quotes.
acs <- read.csv("acs_2023.csv")


# 4. RELATIVE RISK AND THE ODDS RATIO.
#    The groups you compare go in the rows; the outcome goes in
#    the columns. Both variables here are coded 0 and 1.
# CHANGE THIS: your group variable and your outcome variable
insurance_table <- table(Citizen = acs$USCitizen,
                         Insured = acs$HealthInsurance)
insurance_table

       Insured
Citizen    0    1
      0  152  425
      1  736 8687

#    Each group's risk: the proportion in each row with each
#    outcome.
# CHANGE THIS: your table's name
risk <- prop.table(insurance_table, margin = 1)
risk

       Insured
Citizen          0          1
      0 0.26343154 0.73656846
      1 0.07810676 0.92189324


73.7% of noncitizens (row 0) and 92.2% of citizens (row 1) have health insurance (column 1).
Relative risk divides one group’s risk by the baseline group’s risk. Square brackets pick one cell: the row name first, then the column name, each in quotes.

# RELATIVE RISK: one group's risk of the outcome divided by the
# baseline group's risk.
#    risk["0", "1"] means the row named 0 (noncitizens) and the
#      column named 1 (insured). The row comes first, then the
#      column, each in quotes.
# CHANGE THIS: the row of your group, the row of your baseline
#              group, and the column of your outcome
risk["0", "1"] / risk["1", "1"]

[1] 0.7989737


The relative risk is 0.80: noncitizens are 80% as likely as citizens to have health insurance. Using the textbook’s flipping trick, \(1 / 0.80 = 1.25\): citizens are 1.25 times as likely to be insured.
The odds ratio divides one group’s odds by the baseline group’s odds. Each group’s odds is its risk of the outcome divided by its risk of not having it:

# THE ODDS RATIO.
#    Each group's odds: its risk of the outcome divided by its
#      risk of not having it. risk[, "1"] (nothing before the
#      comma) means the whole column named 1, for every row.
# CHANGE THIS: the column of your outcome first, then the other
#              column
odds <- risk[, "1"] / risk[, "0"]
odds

        0         1 
 2.796053 11.802989 

#    The odds ratio: one group's odds divided by the baseline
#    group's odds.
# CHANGE THIS: your group first, then your baseline group
odds["0"] / odds["1"]

        0 
0.2368936 


The first line gives each group’s odds: about 2.8 insured noncitizens for every uninsured one, and about 11.8 for citizens. The odds ratio is 0.24 (the 0 printed above it is just the label of the group it came from).
Cohen’s effect size cutoffs have been translated to the odds ratio scale. Use the column that matches your odds ratio:

In the “Odds ratio < 1.0” column, 0.24 is beyond the 0.29 cutoff for a medium effect but not as far as 0.11 for a large one, so it is a medium effect.






WarningCommon error: subscript out of bounds



What you see

risk["No", "1"]

Error in `[.default`:
! subscript out of bounds


What it means: the table has no row called No. The row and column names must match the table exactly; here they are 0 and 1, because that is how the variables are coded.

TipWith your own data



Put your group variable first in table() and your outcome second. Then, in the relative risk and odds ratio lines, change the names in quotes: your group’s row, your baseline group’s row, and your outcome’s column. If your variables use words instead of 0 and 1, use those words, spelled exactly as in the table.

title: 8  Categorical Data Analysis
text:
8.7 Sensitivity and specificity
Sensitivity and specificity describe how well a yes/no rule predicts what actually happens. In this example, the rule predicts high blood pressure for everyone in the Obese BMI group, and the outcome is a systolic reading of 140 mmHg or higher. Two ifelse() lines create the predicted and actual columns, and table() builds the confusion matrix, with the predictions in the rows:

# CHANGE THIS: the file name of your dataset, inside the quotes.
pressure <- read.csv("smoking_bmi_bp.csv")


# 5. SENSITIVITY AND SPECIFICITY of a yes/no rule.
#    The rule: predict high blood pressure for everyone in the
#      Obese BMI group.
#    What actually happened: a systolic reading of 140 mmHg or
#      higher.
#    == means "is exactly equal to" (two equals signs).
# CHANGE THIS: your rule, your outcome, and new column names
pressure$Predicted <- ifelse(pressure$BMI == "Obese", "Yes", "No")
pressure$Actual <- ifelse(pressure$SystolicBP >= 140, "Yes", "No")

# The confusion matrix: predictions in the rows, what actually
# happened in the columns.
# CHANGE THIS: your dataset name, in both places
confusion <- table(Predicted = pressure$Predicted,
                   Actual = pressure$Actual)
confusion

         Actual
Predicted  No Yes
      No  167 129
      Yes  80 124


Then divide the cells:

# SENSITIVITY: of the people who actually had the outcome, the
# proportion the rule caught.
#    sum(confusion[, "Yes"]) adds up the whole "Yes" column.
# You do not need to change these lines if your labels are Yes
# and No.
confusion["Yes", "Yes"] / sum(confusion[, "Yes"])

[1] 0.4901186

# SPECIFICITY: of the people who did not have the outcome, the
# proportion the rule correctly left alone.
confusion["No", "No"] / sum(confusion[, "No"])

[1] 0.6761134



Sensitivity is 0.49: of the 253 people who actually had high blood pressure, the rule caught 124, or 49%.
Specificity is 0.68: of the 247 people who did not, the rule correctly left 167 alone, or 68%.

The rule misses about half of the people with high blood pressure, so on its own, BMI category is a weak screening rule for it.






TipWith your own data



Write your rule in the first ifelse() and your outcome in the second. Comparisons you can use include == (equal to), >= (at least), > (greater than), <= (at most), and < (less than). If your data already have a predicted column and an actual column, skip the ifelse() lines and put those columns in table(), predictions first.

9.1 The data
This chapter fits the logistic regression models from Chapter 9 of the textbook and gets the values the textbook uses to judge them: odds ratios with confidence intervals, VIF, predicted probabilities, deviance \(R^2\), the Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test, a confusion matrix, and an ROC curve with its AUC. The variables used in this chapter:

title: 9  Logistic Regression
text:
9.3 Simple logistic regression
glm() takes the outcome before the ~ and the predictor after it, like lm(). Two extra arguments make it a logistic regression that handles missing values:

# 1. SIMPLE LOGISTIC REGRESSION.
#    glm() is written like lm(): the outcome before the ~, the
#      predictor after it.
#    family = binomial makes it a logistic regression (for a 0/1
#      outcome). Leave it as is.
#    na.action = na.exclude skips rows with missing values but
#      keeps their places, so the predictions line up with the
#      dataset later. Leave it as is.
# CHANGE THIS: your outcome, your predictor, your dataset, and a
#              name for your model
age_model <- glm(smoke ~ age4, data = youth, family = binomial,
                 na.action = na.exclude)
summary(age_model)


Call:
glm(formula = smoke ~ age4, family = binomial, data = youth, 
    na.action = na.exclude)

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept) -3.68798    0.24027  -15.35   <2e-16 ***
age4         0.23686    0.01485   15.95   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 17890  on 12947  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 17631  on 12946  degrees of freedom
  (439 observations deleted due to missingness)
AIC: 17635

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4

# The odds ratios: exp() turns each slope into an odds ratio.
# CHANGE THIS: your model's name
exp(coef(age_model))

(Intercept)        age4 
 0.02502241  1.26726184 


The Coefficients table has the same columns as the textbook’s Table 9.1, apart from the odds ratios, which come next. Read it in two steps:

The slope’s sign and p-value. The Estimate for age4 is 0.237, a log-odds slope: positive, so older students were more likely to have tried smoking, p < .001.
The odds ratio. exp(coef()) turns each slope into an odds ratio. For age4 it is 1.267: each extra year of age multiplies the odds of having tried smoking by 1.27, a 26.7% increase in the odds. Ignore the (Intercept) odds ratio.

The line (439 observations deleted due to missingness) tells you how many students were left out because they were missing the outcome or the predictor.






NoteCheck: the family line



Look for (Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1) near the bottom of the output. If it says gaussian instead, you left out family = binomial, and R fit an ordinary regression without any error or warning. Add the argument and run the model again.

9.4 Multiple logistic regression
List the predictors after the ~, joined with + signs, as in Chapter 5:

# 2. MULTIPLE LOGISTIC REGRESSION: list the predictors after the

youth_model <- glm(smoke ~ ride.alc.driver + age4, data = youth,
                   family = binomial, na.action = na.exclude)

    data = youth, na.action = na.exclude)

Both predictors are significant, p < .001, each while holding the other constant. For the odds ratios with their 95% confidence intervals, in the layout of the textbook’s Table 9.4:

# Odds ratios with their 95% confidence intervals, side by side.
#    confint.default() gives the confidence intervals for the
#      slopes; exp() turns everything into odds ratios.
#    cbind() puts the columns side by side; OR = names the first.

# CHANGE THIS: your model's name, in both places

                confint.default(youth_model))), 4)

age4: each extra year of age multiplies the odds by 1.26 (a 26% increase), 95% CI [1.22, 1.30], for students with the same answer about riding with a drinking driver.


# VIF, as in Chapter 5.
# CHANGE THIS: your model's name
vif(youth_model)

ride.alc.driver            age4 
       1.000369        1.000369 


Both VIFs are 1.00, so the predictors do not overlap.






Noteconfint() or confint.default()?



confint.default() gives Wald intervals, the kind most statistics programs report (and the textbook uses). You may see confint() in other R guides. It uses a different method that refits the model many times to find each interval’s ends; the message Waiting for profiling to be done... only means R is doing that work. Its intervals are a little more accurate in small samples. With a large sample, the two agree closely; use confint.default() to match the textbook.

Change the outcome, the predictors, the dataset, and the model’s name. Use the model’s name in the odds ratio and VIF lines too. A categorical predictor stored as words works as in Chapter 5: R makes the indicator variables and names each row after its group.

title: 9  Logistic Regression
text:
9.5 Predicted probabilities
To predict the probability for specific people, build a small table of profiles with data.frame(). It needs one column for each predictor, named exactly as in the model:

# 3. PREDICTED PROBABILITIES for specific profiles.
#    data.frame() builds a small table of profiles: one column per
#      predictor, spelled exactly as in the model, one row per
#      profile. Here: two 16-year-olds, one who did not ride with
#      a drinking driver (0) and one who did (1).
# CHANGE THIS: your predictors and the values for each profile
profiles <- data.frame(ride.alc.driver = c(0, 1),
                       age4 = c(16, 16))

#    type = "response" gives probabilities (0 to 1) instead of
#    log-odds. Leave it as is.
# CHANGE THIS: your model's name
predict(youth_model, newdata = profiles, type = "response")

        1         2 
0.4410983 0.7153773 


A 16-year-old who had not ridden with a drinking driver has a predicted probability of 0.44 (44%) of having tried smoking; a 16-year-old who had has a probability of 0.72 (72%). The 1 and 2 above the probabilities are the row numbers of the profiles.






TipWith your own data



Give data.frame() one column per predictor, using the predictor names from your model, and list one value per profile inside each c(). Every column needs the same number of values. For a categorical predictor stored as words, type the group name in quotes, such as Group = c("Control", "Treatment").

title: 9  Logistic Regression
text:
9.6 Deviance R-squared
R does not print the deviance \(R^2\), but it stores the pieces needed to calculate it. The first line gives the deviance \(R^2\), and the second the adjusted deviance \(R^2\):

# 4. DEVIANCE R-SQUARED: how much the model reduced the deviance,
#    compared with a model with no predictors.
#    $deviance is the model's deviance; $null.deviance is the
#      deviance with no predictors.
#    $df.residual and $df.null are their degrees of freedom,
#      which the adjusted version uses.
# CHANGE THIS: your model's name (in every place on both lines)
1 - youth_model$deviance / youth_model$null.deviance

[1] 0.06125779

1 - (youth_model$deviance / youth_model$df.residual) /
  (youth_model$null.deviance / youth_model$df.null)

[1] 0.06111275


The model reduced the deviance by 6.1% compared with a model with no predictors (adjusted deviance \(R^2\) also 6.1%, since the sample is large). The predictors are significant, but they leave most of the deviance unexplained, the same pattern the textbook describes for its ICU model.

title: 9  Logistic Regression
text:
9.7 Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test
The Hosmer-Lemeshow test sorts the people into groups by their predicted probability and compares how many 1s each group actually had with how many the model predicted. Some software also reports a deviance goodness-of-fit test, but its p-value is unreliable when each combination of predictor values belongs to only a few people; grouping lets Hosmer-Lemeshow hold up in that situation. As the textbook explains, its hypotheses run backward: a large p-value means you have no evidence that the model fits poorly.

# 5. HOSMER-LEMESHOW TEST, from the DescTools package.
#    DescTools:: tells R which package the function comes from,
#      so you do not need a library() line for it.
#    fit = the predicted probabilities, and obs = the actual 0/1
#      outcomes, for the people the model used. The model stores
#      both: $fitted.values and $y.
#    $C keeps the standard version of the test (the function also
#      calculates a second version, $H).
# CHANGE THIS: your model's name (in both places), and a name for
#              the result
hl <- DescTools::HosmerLemeshowTest(fit = youth_model$fitted.values,
                                    obs = youth_model$y)$C

Warning in DescTools::HosmerLemeshowTest(fit =
youth_model$fitted.values, : Found only 8 different groups for
Hosmer-Lemesho C statistic.

hl


    Hosmer-Lemeshow C statistic

data:  youth_model$fitted.values and youth_model$y
X-squared = 12.715, df = 6, p-value = 0.0478


The result: \(\chi^2(6) = 12.72\), p = .048. Taken alone, that p-value is just below .05, evidence that the model does not fit well.






NoteWarning: Found only 8 different groups



The test normally uses 10 groups. This model has only two predictors with few values (0 or 1, and five ages), so it gives only 10 different predicted probabilities, and some of them are too close together to split into 10 groups. R uses the 8 groups it can make, lowers the degrees of freedom to match (8 − 2 = 6), and tells you so. The warning does not mean anything went wrong. (The misspelling “Hosmer-Lemesho” is R’s.)



9.7.1 A large sample makes small differences significant
Before you conclude that the model fits badly, look at how big the differences are. The first line gives the share of students in each group who actually had tried smoking, and the second the share the model predicted:

# The share of 1s in each group: what actually happened, then what
# the model predicted.
#    prop.table(..., margin = 1) turns each row into proportions,
#      as in Chapter 2; [, 2] keeps the column for the 1s.
# CHANGE THIS: your result's name, in both lines
round(prop.table(hl$observed, margin = 1)[, 2], 2)

[0.332,0.385] (0.385,0.441] (0.441,0.499] (0.499,0.556] 
         0.37          0.46          0.50          0.53 
(0.556,0.613] (0.613,0.715]  (0.715,0.76]    (0.76,0.8] 
         0.57          0.69          0.78          0.79 

round(prop.table(hl$expected, margin = 1)[, 2], 2)

[0.332,0.385] (0.385,0.441] (0.441,0.499] (0.499,0.556] 
         0.37          0.44          0.50          0.56 
(0.556,0.613] (0.613,0.715]  (0.715,0.76]    (0.76,0.8] 
         0.61          0.69          0.76          0.80 


Each label is the range of predicted probabilities in that group, such as (0.499,0.556] for students the model gave a 50% to 56% chance. In every group, the model’s prediction is within about 4 percentage points of what happened (for example, 0.53 actual and 0.56 predicted in the fourth group). With 12,948 students, the test is powerful enough to call even differences this small significant. This is the textbook’s warning about sample size and practical significance: a p-value measures the strength of the evidence, not the size of the problem. With a large sample, report the test, and judge the fit by comparing the two lines as well.






TipWith your own data



Change the model’s name in both places in the HosmerLemeshowTest() line. If your model has a continuous predictor (as the textbook’s ICU model has age), you will get the full 10 groups and 8 degrees of freedom, and no warning.

title: 9  Logistic Regression
text:
9.8 Confusion matrix
fitted() gives each student’s predicted probability. Store it as a new column, turn it into a 0/1 prediction with a 50% threshold, and cross-tabulate the predictions against what actually happened:

# 6. CONFUSION MATRIX.
#    fitted() gives each person's predicted probability; store it
#      as a new column.
#    ifelse(... > 0.5, 1, 0) predicts 1 when the probability is
#      over 50% (the threshold), and 0 otherwise.
# CHANGE THIS: your dataset, your model, and (if you want a
#              different threshold) the 0.5
youth$prob <- fitted(youth_model)
youth$predicted <- ifelse(youth$prob > 0.5, 1, 0)

# Predictions in the rows, what actually happened in the columns.
# CHANGE THIS: your dataset and your outcome
confusion <- table(Predicted = youth$predicted,
                   Actual = youth$smoke)
confusion

         Actual
Predicted    0    1
        0 4295 3298
        1 1741 3614

# Sensitivity and specificity, as in Chapter 8. You do not need
# to change these lines if your outcome is coded 0 and 1.
confusion["1", "1"] / sum(confusion[, "1"])

[1] 0.5228588

confusion["0", "0"] / sum(confusion[, "0"])

[1] 0.7115639


At the 50% threshold, the model’s sensitivity is 0.52 (it caught 52% of the students who had tried smoking) and its specificity is 0.71 (it correctly identified 71% of those who had not). To try a different threshold, as the textbook describes, change the 0.5 in the ifelse() line and run the lines below it again.






WarningCommon error: replacement has 12948 rows, data has 13387



What you see

no_exclude <- glm(smoke ~ ride.alc.driver + age4, data = youth,
                  family = binomial)
youth$prob <- fitted(no_exclude)

Error in `$<-.data.frame`:
! replacement has 12948 rows, data has 13387


What it means: without na.action = na.exclude, the model leaves out the rows with missing values completely, so it has fewer predictions than the dataset has rows.
How to fix it: add na.action = na.exclude inside glm() and fit the model again. The missing rows then get NA as their prediction, and the column fits.








WarningCommon error: subscript out of bounds



What you see

strict <- table(Predicted = ifelse(youth$prob > 0.9, 1, 0),
                Actual = youth$smoke)
strict

         Actual
Predicted    0    1
        0 6036 6912

strict["1", "1"] / sum(strict[, "1"])

Error in `[.default`:
! subscript out of bounds


What it means: no student has a predicted probability over 0.9, so every prediction is 0 and the table has no row named 1. The same thing happens at the 50% threshold when the outcome is rare or very common, as with the textbook’s ICU model, where nearly everyone is predicted to survive.
How to fix it: print the confusion matrix before calculating. If it has only one row, the rule never predicts the other outcome; try a threshold closer to the middle of the predicted probabilities.

title: 9  Logistic Regression
text:
9.9 ROC curve and AUC
roc() compares the actual outcomes with the predicted probabilities at every possible threshold, and auc() gives the area under the curve:

# 7. ROC CURVE AND AUC.
#    roc(actual, predicted) compares what happened with the
#      predicted probabilities, at every possible threshold.
# CHANGE THIS: your outcome and your predicted probabilities
youth_roc <- roc(youth$smoke, youth$prob)

Setting levels: control = 0, case = 1


Setting direction: controls < cases

auc(youth_roc)

Area under the curve: 0.6598


The AUC is 0.66. On the common grading scale, that is above 0.50 (guessing) but below the 0.70 that counts as acceptable.






NoteMessages: Setting levels and Setting direction



roc() reports which outcome it treated as the event (case = 1) and that the event should have the higher predicted probabilities. Both are what you want for a 0/1 outcome, so you can ignore the messages.


Draw the ROC curve with ggroc(), which makes a ggplot:

# The ROC curve.
#    ggroc() draws it as a ggplot, so the usual + layers work.
#    legacy.axes = TRUE puts the false positive rate (1 minus
#      specificity) along the bottom, the usual way to draw an ROC
#      curve. Leave it as is.
#    geom_abline() adds the diagonal "coin flip" line: intercept
#      = 0 and slope = 1 start it at the corner and run it at 45
#      degrees. linetype = "dashed" makes it dashed.
# CHANGE THIS: your ROC object's name and your title
ggroc(youth_roc, legacy.axes = TRUE, color = "#0072B2",
      linewidth = 1) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "ROC Curve: Predicting Ever Smoking",
       x = "False positive rate (1 - specificity)",
       y = "Sensitivity") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)




ROC curve for the logistic regression of ever smoking on riding with a drinking driver and age.




The curve bows above the dashed “coin flip” diagonal, but not far toward the top-left corner, which matches the modest AUC.






TipWith your own data



Put your outcome and your predicted probability column inside roc(), then change the name inside auc() and ggroc(), and update the title.

title: 10  Nonparametric Tests

All five are built into R, so there are no packages to load. Report the medians and the effect size alongside each test, since the test alone does not show which group is higher or by how much, so every section starts with them.

title: 10  Nonparametric Tests
text:
10.2 Wilcoxon signed-rank test
The question: did participants keep their weight off between month 4 and month 7? Each participant has both measurements, so they are paired.
Some participants are missing one of the two measurements. Keep only the people with both, so the medians and the test use the same people:

# CHANGE THIS: the file name of your dataset, inside the quotes.
weight <- read.csv("weight_loss_incentive.csv")


# 1. WILCOXON SIGNED-RANK test.
#    Keep only the people with BOTH measurements, using subset()
#    from Chapter 3. !is.na() means "is not missing", and & means
#    "and".
# CHANGE THIS: your dataset and your two paired measurements
pairs <- subset(weight, !is.na(WeightLoss) & !is.na(Month7Loss))
nrow(pairs)

[1] 32


32 participants have both measurements. Then the medians:

# The descriptive statistics: each measurement's median and the
# median of the differences (first minus second).
# CHANGE THIS: your two paired measurements
median(pairs$WeightLoss)

[1] 7.5

median(pairs$Month7Loss)

[1] 6

median(pairs$WeightLoss - pairs$Month7Loss)

[1] 4.75


The median weight loss was 7.5 pounds at month 4 and 6 pounds at month 7, and the median difference (month 4 minus month 7) was 4.75 pounds. Then the test, with paired = TRUE:

# The test.
#    paired = TRUE pairs the two measurements row by row.
#    exact = FALSE makes R use the normal approximation, which
#      the effect size below needs. correct = FALSE matches the
#      textbook's results. Leave them as they are.
#    The second line prints the saved result.
# CHANGE THIS: your two paired measurements, in the same order as
#              above, and a name for the result
weight_test <- wilcox.test(pairs$WeightLoss, pairs$Month7Loss,
                           paired = TRUE, exact = FALSE,
                           correct = FALSE)
weight_test


    Wilcoxon signed rank test

data:  pairs$WeightLoss and pairs$Month7Loss
V = 311, p-value = 0.3794
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0



Where each Wilcoxon value appears in R’s output


What you report
Where it is in the output
In this example




Test statistic, \(W\)
V
311


p-value
p-value
.379


Effect size, \(r\)
calculated below
.16



The p-value is far above .05, so the difference between month 4 and month 7 is not statistically significant.
R does not print the effect size, Rosenthal’s \(r\). These lines calculate it from the p-value, with \(n\) as the number of pairs:

# The effect size, Rosenthal's r (R does not print it).
#    qnorm() turns the test's p-value back into its z-value.
#    abs() drops the minus sign; sqrt() is the square root.
# Copy these lines as they are; change only the result's name and
# n, the number of pairs.
z <- qnorm(weight_test$p.value / 2)
n <- 32
abs(z) / sqrt(n)

[1] 0.1553976


\(r = .16\), a small effect.






TipWith your own data



Change the dataset and the two measurements in subset(), the median() lines, and wilcox.test(), then the result’s name and n in the effect size lines. Keep the two measurements in the same order everywhere, so the differences all subtract the same way.

title: 10  Nonparametric Tests
text:
10.3 Mann-Whitney U test
The question: do female and male students send different numbers of texts? Text counts are very skewed (most students send a few dozen a day, and one reported 1,000), so the medians tell the story better than the means.

# CHANGE THIS: the file name of your dataset, inside the quotes.
students <- read.csv("census_at_school.csv")


# 2. MANN-WHITNEY U test.
#    Each group's median, with tapply() from Chapter 3.
# CHANGE THIS: your numerical variable and your group variable
tapply(students$TextsSent, students$Gender, median)

Female   Male 
    30     20 

#    The test is written like t.test(): the numerical variable
#    before the ~, the group variable after it. The other
#    settings work as in the Wilcoxon test above.
# CHANGE THIS: your numerical variable, your group variable,
#              your dataset, and a name for the result
texts_test <- wilcox.test(TextsSent ~ Gender, data = students,
                          exact = FALSE, correct = FALSE)
texts_test


    Wilcoxon rank sum test

data:  TextsSent by Gender
W = 38178, p-value = 1.497e-05
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0


The median female student sent 30 texts the previous day; the median male student sent 20. The test: \(U = 38178\), p < .001. The medians show the direction: female students sent more texts. Then the effect size, calculated the same way as for the Wilcoxon test, with \(n\) as the number of people in both groups together:

# The effect size, Rosenthal's r, the same way as above.
# Copy these lines as they are; change only the result's name and
# n, the number of people in both groups together.
z <- qnorm(texts_test$p.value / 2)
n <- 500
abs(z) / sqrt(n)

[1] 0.1936068


\(r = .19\), a small effect: the difference is real, but the two groups overlap a great deal.






NoteR calls it W



R labels the statistic W, but its value is the \(U\) statistic that the textbook reports. As the textbook explains, different programs use different labels for this test’s statistic.








WarningCommon error: grouping factor must have exactly 2 levels



What you see

wilcox.test(TextsSent ~ GetToSchool, data = students)

Error in `wilcox.test.formula()`:
! grouping factor must have exactly 2 levels


What it means: GetToSchool has three groups, and the Mann-Whitney test compares exactly two.
How to fix it: for three or more groups, use the Kruskal-Wallis test below. To compare just two of the groups, keep those two with subset() and %in%, as in Chapter 6.








TipWith your own data



Change the numerical variable, the group variable, and the dataset in both lines, then the result’s name and n in the effect size lines.

title: 10  Nonparametric Tests
text:
10.4 Kruskal-Wallis test
The question: do students who feel different amounts of school pressure spend different amounts of time on homework? First put the groups in order, as in Chapter 6, and look at each group’s size and median:

# 3. KRUSKAL-WALLIS test.
#    Put the groups in order, as in Chapter 6.
# CHANGE THIS: your group variable (in both places) and your
#              groups, in order
students$SchoolPressure <- factor(students$SchoolPressure,
  levels = c("None", "Very little", "Some", "A lot"))

#    Each group's size and median.
# CHANGE THIS: your numerical variable and your group variable
table(students$SchoolPressure)


       None Very little        Some       A lot 
         26         100         241         133 

tapply(students$HWHours, students$SchoolPressure, median)

       None Very little        Some       A lot 
       0.25        2.00        5.00        5.00 


The medians rise from 0.25 hours a week for students who feel no pressure to 5 hours for those who feel some or a lot. Then the test:

# The test, written like aov() in Chapter 6.
# CHANGE THIS: your numerical variable, your group variable,
#              your dataset, and a name for the result
pressure_test <- kruskal.test(HWHours ~ SchoolPressure,
                              data = students)
pressure_test


    Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test

data:  HWHours by SchoolPressure
Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 101.29, df = 3, p-value <
2.2e-16


R labels the \(H\) statistic Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared, and it is the version adjusted for ties (students with the same value share a rank, and the adjustment accounts for that sharing): \(H(3) = 101.29\), p < .001. Homework time differs across the pressure groups.
R does not print the effect size, epsilon-squared. These lines calculate it from \(H\):

# The effect size, epsilon-squared (R does not print it).
#    $statistic picks out H from the test's results.
# Copy these lines as they are; change only the result's name and
# n, the number of people with both values.
n <- 500
pressure_test$statistic / (n - 1)

Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared 
                 0.2029805 


\(\varepsilon^2 = 0.20\), a large effect: the pressure groups account for about 20% of the variation in homework-time ranks. R prints the label Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared above the number because the value came from that part of the results; the number itself is \(\varepsilon^2\).






TipWith your own data



Change the group variable and its groups in factor(), then the numerical variable, the group variable, and the dataset in table(), tapply(), and kruskal.test(), and the result’s name and n in the effect size lines.

title: 10  Nonparametric Tests
text:
10.5 Spearman’s rho
Spearman’s rho works for an ordered categorical variable, such as school pressure, because it uses only the ranks. Unlike Kruskal-Wallis, which treats the groups as separate buckets, it uses their order, which gives it more power. To use the groups in a correlation, first turn them into ranks with as.integer(), which gives each group its place in the order you set. Then run cor.test() from Chapter 4 with method = "spearman":

# 4. SPEARMAN'S RHO.
#    For an ordered categorical variable, first turn its groups
#    into ranks: as.integer() gives each group its place in the
#    order set above (None = 1, Very little = 2, Some = 3,
#    A lot = 4). Skip this line if both variables are numerical.
# CHANGE THIS: your ordered variable and a name for its ranks
students$PressureRank <- as.integer(students$SchoolPressure)

#    method = "spearman" makes cor.test() from Chapter 4 calculate
#      Spearman's rho instead of Pearson's r.
#    exact = FALSE is needed when values are tied, as they almost
#      always are. Leave it as is.
# CHANGE THIS: your two variables, and a name for the result
pressure_rho <- cor.test(students$HWHours, students$PressureRank,
                         method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
pressure_rho


    Spearman's rank correlation rho

data:  students$HWHours and students$PressureRank
S = 12529669, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
sample estimates:
      rho 
0.3985735 


\(r_s = .40\), p < .001: students who feel more school pressure tend to spend more time on homework. Ignore the S statistic; it is a step in calculating the p-value, while \(r_s\) is the number your reader can interpret.
R does not print a confidence interval for Spearman’s rho. These three lines calculate one with the usual method (Fisher’s \(z\) transformation):

# The 95% confidence interval for rho (R does not print one).
# Copy these lines as they are; change only the result's name and
# n, the number of people with both values (with no missing
# values, the number of rows in your dataset).
rho <- pressure_rho$estimate
n <- 500
tanh(atanh(rho) + c(-1.96, 1.96) / sqrt(n - 3))

[1] 0.3221407 0.4698438


The 95% CI is [.32, .47].






TipWith your own data



If both of your variables are numerical, skip the as.integer() line and put your two variables straight into cor.test(). If one is an ordered categorical variable, set its order with factor() first, so the ranks go from lowest to highest.

title: 10  Nonparametric Tests
text:
10.6 Fisher’s exact test
Chapter 8 of this companion showed that the chi-square test for gender and travel to school gives the warning Chi-squared approximation may be incorrect, because few students walk. Fisher’s exact test handles small expected counts, because it has no minimum expected count:

# 5. FISHER'S EXACT test, for a cross-tabulation with expected
#    counts below 5 (see Chapter 8).
#    Row proportions first, as in Chapter 2, to see the pattern.
# CHANGE THIS: your two categorical variables
travel_table <- table(students$Gender, students$GetToSchool)
travel_table

        
         Bus Car Walk
  Female  20 236    4
  Male    35 202    3

round(prop.table(travel_table, margin = 1), 3)

        
           Bus   Car  Walk
  Female 0.077 0.908 0.015
  Male   0.146 0.842 0.013

# The test needs only the table.
# CHANGE THIS: your table's name
fisher.test(travel_table)


    Fisher's Exact Test for Count Data

data:  travel_table
p-value = 0.04274
alternative hypothesis: two.sided


Fisher’s exact test has no test statistic, so report the proportions and the p-value: 14.6% of male students and 7.7% of female students take the bus to school, and the test finds the travel pattern differs by gender, p = .043.






TipWith your own data



Change the two variables in table(). fisher.test() works on a 2 × 2 table or a larger one, as here.

title: 11  Factor Analysis
text:
11.1 The data
This chapter follows the factor analysis workflow from Chapter 11 of the textbook: look at the correlation matrix, choose the number of factors with a scree chart, extract and rotate the factors, read the factor matrix, and check each factor’s items with Cronbach’s alpha.
Get the script: Download the Chapter 11 script, chapter_11.R, and save it in the same folder as your data.
Download amas_math_anxiety.csv into the same folder as the script. It holds answers from 2,200 adults to the nine-item Abbreviated Math Anxiety Scale (AMAS), which you used for Cronbach’s alpha in Chapter 2. The question in this chapter: do the nine items measure one kind of math anxiety, or more than one?
The variables used in this chapter:
The data key describes the situation behind each item. Keep it open as you read the results: naming the factors means reading what their items have in common.

section: 11.2 Load the packages and the data
text:
11.2 Load the packages and the data
This chapter uses ggplot2 for the scree chart and psych for the factor analysis and Cronbach’s alpha. If either is not installed yet, go back to Install and load packages in Getting Set Up.

# ggplot2 draws the scree chart; psych runs the factor analysis
# and Cronbach's alpha.
library(ggplot2)
library(psych)


Attaching package: 'psych'


The following objects are masked from 'package:ggplot2':

    %+%, alpha


The message about %+% and alpha is the one explained in Chapter 2, and you can ignore it.
A factor analysis uses every column you give it, so keep only the survey items. This file holds nothing but the nine items, but most datasets have other columns too, so the script shows how to pick the items out:

# CHANGE THIS: the file name of your dataset, inside the quotes.
amas <- read.csv("amas_math_anxiety.csv")

# Keep only the survey items, as in Chapter 2.
#    amas[, c(...)] keeps every row (nothing before the comma)
#    and only the columns named inside c().
# CHANGE THIS: your dataset and the names of your items
items <- amas[, c("item_1", "item_2", "item_3", "item_4",
                  "item_5", "item_6", "item_7", "item_8",
                  "item_9")]

What you see

students <- read.csv("census_at_school.csv")
cor(students)

Error in `cor()`:
! 'x' must be numeric


What it means: the dataset includes columns that are not numbers (such as Gender), and a correlation needs numbers.

11.4 Scree chart
The eigenvalues measure how much variation each potential factor explains, largest first. Store them in a small dataset with the factor numbers and plot them:

# 2. SCREE CHART.
#    eigen(cor(items))$values gives the amount of variation each
#      potential factor explains (its eigenvalue), largest first.
#    1:9 means the whole numbers from 1 to 9, one per item.
# CHANGE THIS: the 9 in 1:9, to your number of items
eigenvalues <- eigen(cor(items))$values
scree <- data.frame(Factor = 1:9, Eigenvalue = eigenvalues)
round(scree, 2)

  Factor Eigenvalue
1      1       5.68
2      2       1.19
3      3       0.50
4      4       0.35
5      5       0.33
6      6       0.31

#    geom_line() joins the points; geom_point() marks them.
#    scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:9) labels every factor number.

  geom_line(color = "#0072B2", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2", size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:9) +

title: 11  Factor Analysis
text:
11.5 Factor analysis
fa() from the psych package runs the factor analysis. Set the number of factors from the scree chart, fm = "pa" for principal axis factoring, and rotate = "varimax" for varimax rotation:

# 3. FACTOR ANALYSIS with fa() from psych.
#    nfactors = 2 is the number of factors to extract (from the
#      scree chart).
#    fm = "pa" means principal axis factoring.
#    rotate = "varimax" means varimax rotation.
# CHANGE THIS: the number of factors, and a name for the result
paf <- fa(items, nfactors = 2, fm = "pa", rotate = "varimax")

# The rotated factor matrix.
#    cutoff = 0 prints every loading (by default, R hides small
#      ones).
#    sort = TRUE lists the items grouped by the factor they load
#      on most.
# CHANGE THIS: your result's name
print(paf$loadings, cutoff = 0, sort = TRUE)


Loadings:
       PA1   PA2  
item_1 0.644 0.287
item_3 0.735 0.383
item_6 0.842 0.263
item_7 0.819 0.271
item_9 0.695 0.453
item_2 0.344 0.794
item_4 0.293 0.861
item_5 0.406 0.693
item_8 0.257 0.791

Proportion Var 0.361 0.339
Cumulative Var 0.361 0.701


The output matches the layout of the textbook’s Table 11.2, with the factors labeled PA1 and PA2:

Loadings. With sort = TRUE, the items are grouped by the factor they load on most. Items 1, 3, 6, 7, and 9 load on PA1 (0.64 to 0.84), and items 2, 4, 5, and 8 load on PA2 (0.69 to 0.86). Using the common 0.40 benchmark (a loading of 0.40 or more makes an item a meaningful member of a factor), two items also load on the other factor: item 9 (0.45 on PA2) and item 5 (0.41 on PA1). Each still loads much more strongly on its own factor, but the structure is not perfectly simple.
Naming the factors. The PA1 items are about learning math (lectures, the board, a new chapter); the PA2 items are about being evaluated (tests, quizzes, a difficult homework load). These match the AMAS’s two published parts, learning anxiety and evaluation anxiety.
Proportion Var is each factor’s share of the total variance: 36.1% for PA1 and 33.9% for PA2. Cumulative Var shows the total, 70.1%.

text:
11.6 Cronbach’s alpha for each factor
Finally, check each factor’s items with Cronbach’s alpha before you combine them into a score, as in Chapter 2:

# 5. CRONBACH'S ALPHA for the items in each factor, as in
#    Chapter 2.
#    psych::alpha() makes sure R uses the alpha() from psych (see
#      Chapter 2).
#    $total$raw_alpha keeps just Cronbach's alpha from the results.
# CHANGE THIS: the items that loaded on each factor
psych::alpha(items[, c("item_1", "item_3", "item_6", "item_7",
                       "item_9")])$total$raw_alpha

Both factors are reliable: 0.91 for the learning items and 0.91 for the evaluation items, well above the 0.70 threshold. You can now build a composite score for each factor with rowSums(), as in Chapter 2.
